Salty snack brands.Pringles: Pringles are made from a dough and stacked in a tube; their saddle shape is a hyperbolic paraboloid, which keeps them from breaking.
Salty snack brands.Doritos: Doritos, launched in 1964 at Disneyland, were created from leftover tortillas that were fried and seasoned for the park.
Salty snack brands.Cheetos: Cheetos leave a bright orange dust on fingers, and it is so famous that the cheese dust has its own nickname, Cheeto dust.
Salty snack brands.Lay's: Lay's is sold as Walkers in the UK, and as Frito-Lay's flagship it is among the world's best-selling potato chips.
Salty snack brands.Ritz: Ritz crackers launched in 1934 in the middle of the Great Depression, as an affordable luxury.
Salty snack brands.Goldfish: Goldfish crackers were inspired by the wife of Pepperidge Farm's founder, who liked the fish she saw on a trip to Switzerland.
Salty snack brands.Fritos: Fritos began in 1932 when Charles Doolin bought a corn chip recipe for 100 dollars from a Mexican man in San Antonio.
Salty snack brands.Tostitos: Tostitos is a Frito-Lay brand that popularized the scoop-shaped chip made for dipping into salsa.
Salty snack brands.Ruffles: Ruffles' ridges made the chips sturdy enough for thick dips, and the brand's slogan is 'Ruffles have ridges'.
Salty snack brands.Walkers: Walkers is Britain's Lay's, a crisp brand from Leicester that began as a pork butcher's shop in 1948.
Salty snack brands.Funyuns: Funyuns are onion-flavored corn rings from 1969, and they contain no real onion rings, just corn meal and flavoring.
Salty snack brands.Takis: Takis are rolled, spicy tortilla chips from Mexico, and their chili-lime dust turns fingers a bright red.
Salty snack brands.Cheez-It: Cheez-It crackers date to 1921 and are cooked in square form, with a hole in the middle for steam to escape.
Salty snack brands.Oreo: Oreo is a sweet cookie, not a salty snack, and since 1912 it has been the world's best-selling cookie.
Salty snack brands.Skittles: Skittles are sweet, fruit-flavored candies, whose slogan is Taste the Rainbow, so they are not salty.
Salty snack brands.Twix: Twix is a chocolate-coated biscuit and caramel bar, and a sweet snack, from Mars.
Salty snack brands.Twinkies: Twinkies are cream-filled sponge cakes, and a sweet snack that was invented in Illinois in 1930.
Salty snack brands.M&M's: M&M's are sweet chocolate candies, and the name comes from the founders Mars and Murrie.
Salty snack brands.Hershey's: Hershey's is best known for chocolate, a sweet treat, so it doesn't fit among salty snacks.
Salty snack brands.Starburst: Starburst is a fruit chew, a sweet candy, and was originally launched in the UK as Opal Fruits.
Salty snack brands.Nutella: Nutella is a sweet hazelnut and cocoa spread from Italy, and it is a spread, not a salty snack.
Salty snack brands.Pop-Tarts: Pop-Tarts are sweet, frosted toaster pastries from Kellogg's, which rushed them out in 1964 to beat a rival product by Post.
Salty snack brands.Chips Ahoy!: Chips Ahoy! is a sweet chocolate chip cookie, so it fails despite the chips in its name.
Salty snack brands.Haribo: Haribo is a German gummy candy maker, and its sweets are sugary, not salty.

Ways to cut with a knife.Julienne: Matchstick strips about 3 mm thick and several centimeters long; the term appeared in French cookbooks of the 1600s.
Ways to cut with a knife.Brunoise: A tiny dice, about 3 mm per side, made by first cutting julienne strips; it is a standard test of classic French knife skill.
Ways to cut with a knife.Chiffonade: Stacked leaves such as basil are rolled up and sliced into thin ribbons; the name comes from the French for made of rags.
Ways to cut with a knife.Dice: A cube cut, ranging from small to large; recipes commonly mean about 6 mm for small dice and 12 mm for medium.
Ways to cut with a knife.Mince: The finest rough cut, used for garlic and herbs, and more finely cut garlic releases more of its sharp flavor compound, allicin.
Ways to cut with a knife.Batonnet: A stick cut about 6 mm by 6 mm by 6 cm, French for little stick, which is the starting point for French fries and for dicing.
Ways to cut with a knife.Chop: A rough cut without exact shape, and the rocking motion of a chef's knife, with the tip down, is the standard way to do it.
Ways to cut with a knife.Slice: A basic cut that makes flat pieces; a sharp knife slices tomatoes cleanly, while a dull one crushes them.
Ways to cut with a knife.Paysanne: A thin, flat shape, often a square or round piece about 1 cm across and 3 mm thick, whose name means peasant style in French.
Ways to cut with a knife.Allumette: Thinner than batonnet, matchstick-sized: allumette means match in French, and it is the cut for shoestring fries.
Ways to cut with a knife.Tourné: A seven-sided football shape cut from vegetables, traditionally with seven faces; the French name means turned.
Ways to cut with a knife.Bias cut: A slice at a slant, about 45 degrees, which exposes more surface for quick cooking and looks elegant in stir-fry dishes.
Ways to cut with a knife.Sauté: A trap: this is a cooking method, not a cut; the French name means jumped, as in the food jumps when tossed in a pan.
Ways to cut with a knife.Blanch: A cooking technique of brief boiling and an ice bath, not a knife cut; it sets bright green color in vegetables.
Ways to cut with a knife.Braise: A slow cooking method with some liquid in a covered pot, not a cut; it turns tough cuts of meat tender.
Ways to cut with a knife.Poach: Gently cooking in barely simmering liquid; no knife is involved, and poaching a good egg takes water at about 80 degrees Celsius.
Ways to cut with a knife.Flambé: Setting alcohol on fire in a pan, a technique, not a cut; the flames burn off alcohol only partially.
Ways to cut with a knife.Deglaze: Adding liquid to a hot pan to loosen browned bits, the base of pan sauces, and it does not involve cutting.
Ways to cut with a knife.Fold: A gentle mixing technique that preserves air in batters, such as when adding egg whites, not a knife cut.
Ways to cut with a knife.Whisk: A tool and verb for beating air into mixtures; it is not a way to cut with a knife.
Ways to cut with a knife.Knead: Working dough with your hands to build gluten; it is a bread technique, not a cut.
Ways to cut with a knife.Sear: Browning food at high heat to trigger the Maillard reaction; this makes flavor, but does not seal in juices, a common myth.
Ways to cut with a knife.Simmer: Cooking in liquid just below boiling, at around 90 degrees Celsius, and not a knife skill.
Ways to cut with a knife.Baste: Spooning fat or juices over food as it cooks to keep it moist; it is a technique, not a cut.

Sandwiches.Reuben: Corned beef, Swiss, sauerkraut and Russian dressing on grilled rye. Its origin is disputed between Omaha and New York City.
Sandwiches.BLT: Bacon, lettuce and tomato on toast. It became hugely popular in postwar America, when bacon and supermarket produce were everywhere.
Sandwiches.Club sandwich: A triple-decker with toasted bread, turkey and bacon, held together with toothpicks. Possibly from a New York club in the 1890s.
Sandwiches.Cuban: Roast pork, ham, Swiss, pickles and mustard pressed on Cuban bread. Both Miami and Tampa claim it, and Tampa famously adds salami.
Sandwiches.Banh mi: Vietnam's baguette sandwich is a legacy of French colonial rule, filled with pickled vegetables, cilantro and pâté or pork.
Sandwiches.Croque monsieur: A French toasted ham and cheese sandwich with béchamel, whose name means 'crunch mister'. Top it with an egg and it becomes a croque madame.
Sandwiches.Po' boy: New Orleans sandwich on crusty French bread, filled with fried shrimp or roast beef. It dates to a 1929 streetcar strike, when it fed 'poor boys'.
Sandwiches.Monte Cristo: A ham-and-cheese sandwich dipped in egg batter and fried, usually served dusted with sugar and jam. It's a French-style sandwich.
Sandwiches.Muffuletta: A New Orleans Italian-American sandwich of cold cuts, cheese and olive salad on a round sesame loaf. The olive spread is its signature.
Sandwiches.Panini: In Italy, 'panini' is the plural of panino, a sandwich. A pressed, grilled sandwich is just one kind.
Sandwiches.Grilled cheese: Cheese between buttered bread, toasted until melted. In the United States it became a school-lunch staple in the 1920s and 30s.
Sandwiches.Sloppy Joe: Ground beef in a tangy tomato sauce on a bun. Its messy filling is meant to spill out.
Sandwiches.Tuna melt: Tuna salad topped with melted cheese and grilled. It's a diner classic that combines two comfort foods.
Sandwiches.Taco: A folded tortilla with filling, not between bread slices. Tacos are a Mexican staple with roots in the silver mines of the 18th century.
Sandwiches.Burrito: A flour tortilla wrapped around its fillings. The name means 'little donkey', and it's a wrap, not a sandwich.
Sandwiches.Quesadilla: A tortilla folded over cheese and griddled. Similar to grilled cheese, but folded tortilla means it is a flatbread dish.
Sandwiches.Calzone: A pizza dough turnover, sealed around its filling. The Italian name means 'trouser leg', probably from its shape.
Sandwiches.Empanada: A pastry turnover baked or fried with filling, found across Spain and Latin America. The name comes from 'to wrap in bread'.
Sandwiches.Samosa: A spiced triangle of fried pastry from South Asia, with roots in Central Asian 'sanbosag' pastries. It is pastry, not a sandwich.
Sandwiches.Spring roll: Thin wrapper rolled around vegetables or meat, and fried or served fresh. Eaten at the Chinese spring festival, which is the origin of its name.
Sandwiches.Crêpe: A thin French pancake folded around fillings. A crêpe is a pancake and not a sandwich, even when folded.
Sandwiches.Pierogi: Polish filled dumplings made of dough, stuffed with potato, cheese or meat, then boiled and often fried afterward.
Sandwiches.Pizza: A flatbread with toppings, not a sandwich, though a 'pizza sandwich' is a thing. Naples is its home.
Sandwiches.Tostada: A flat fried or toasted tortilla with toppings piled on, whose name means 'toasted'. It is open-faced and not a sandwich.

Birds that can't fly.Penguin: Penguins gave up flight for diving; their dense bones act as ballast, and some species can dive hundreds of metres deep.
Birds that can't fly.Ostrich: The largest and heaviest living bird, it can sprint at about 70 km/h and has just two toes on each foot.
Birds that can't fly.Emu: Australia's tallest bird, it can run about 50 km/h. The male incubates the eggs for around eight weeks without eating.
Birds that can't fly.Kiwi: A chicken-sized flightless bird from New Zealand with nostrils at the tip of its beak, and it lays an egg about a fifth of its body weight.
Birds that can't fly.Cassowary: A tall, dangerous bird of New Guinea and northern Australia. Its inner toe has a dagger-like claw about 12 cm long.
Birds that can't fly.Dodo: A flightless pigeon relative from Mauritius. Sailors and the animals they brought wiped it out within about a century of its discovery.
Birds that can't fly.Kakapo: A rare nocturnal parrot from New Zealand and the world's heaviest. It is nearly extinct, with only about 200 birds alive.
Birds that can't fly.Rhea: A South American cousin of the ostrich. Males build the nest, incubate eggs from several females, and raise the chicks alone.
Birds that can't fly.Takahe: A flightless New Zealand bird thought extinct until it was rediscovered in 1948 in a remote valley.
Birds that can't fly.Moa: Giant flightless birds of New Zealand, the largest standing up to about 3.6 metres tall. Humans hunted them to extinction around 600 years ago.
Birds that can't fly.Puffin: This seabird flies well, beating its wings up to 400 times a minute, and uses them as flippers underwater.
Birds that can't fly.Albatross: Not only can it fly, it can glide for hours; the wandering albatross has the longest wingspan of any bird, about 3.5 metres.
Birds that can't fly.Pelican: A big bird that flies surprisingly well, soaring on thermals with a wingspan that can top 3 metres.
Birds that can't fly.Flamingo: Flamingos fly, often at night and in large flocks. Their pink colour comes from pigments in the shrimp and algae they eat.
Birds that can't fly.Peacock: The male's showy tail train is for display, but peafowl can still fly short distances, mostly up into trees to roost.
Birds that can't fly.Toucan: Its huge bill is light and hollow, and helps it shed body heat. Toucans are weak but real fliers, hopping between treetops.
Birds that can't fly.Seagull: A strong flier that can ride the wind for hours. Gulls even drop shellfish from the air to crack them open.
Birds that can't fly.Duck: Ducks fly well and some migrate thousands of kilometres. Many moult all their flight feathers at once, briefly grounding them.
Birds that can't fly.Hummingbird: The only birds that can fly backward. Their wings beat dozens of times per second, and they can hover in place.
Birds that can't fly.Bat: A trap, since bats fly but they are not birds. They are mammals, the only ones capable of true powered flight.
Birds that can't fly.Swan: Heavy but strong fliers. Whooper and tundra swans migrate long distances, sometimes at high altitudes.
Birds that can't fly.Owl: Owls fly silently thanks to soft, fringed feathers that muffle the sound of air, so they can ambush prey.
Birds that can't fly.Crow: Crows fly strongly and are among the smartest birds, able to use tools and recognise individual human faces.
Birds that can't fly.Parrot: Most parrots fly well. The kakapo is the unusual exception, which makes it the flightless parrot that fits this list.

Nocturnal animals.Owl: An owl's eyes are fixed in their sockets, so it turns its head up to about 270 degrees to look around.
Nocturnal animals.Bat: Bats are the only mammals capable of true flight, and some species eat thousands of mosquitoes in a night.
Nocturnal animals.Hedgehog: Hedgehogs are mostly nocturnal, and they can roll into a ball because of a ring of muscle along their back.
Nocturnal animals.Raccoon: Raccoons are nocturnal and their name comes from an Algonquian word meaning 'one who rubs, scrubs and scratches with its hands'.
Nocturnal animals.Aye-aye: The aye-aye uses a long skinny finger to tap on wood and fish out grubs, a Madagascar habit once considered an omen of death.
Nocturnal animals.Kiwi: Kiwis are flightless and nocturnal, and they have nostrils at the tip of the beak to sniff out worms underground.
Nocturnal animals.Opossum: The Virginia opossum is North America's only marsupial, and it can eat thousands of ticks in a season.
Nocturnal animals.Firefly: Fireflies are actually beetles; they glow at night with a chemical reaction that's almost 100 percent efficient.
Nocturnal animals.Moth: Most moths fly at night, and some navigate by moonlight, which is why artificial lights confuse them.
Nocturnal animals.Badger: Badgers spend the day underground in their setts and come out after dusk to forage for worms.
Nocturnal animals.Tarsier: Tarsiers have eyes so large that each one is bigger than the animal's brain, and they hunt insects in the dark.
Nocturnal animals.Bushbaby: Bushbabies, or galagos, are named for their cries, and they can leap several metres between branches at night.
Nocturnal animals.Squirrel: Squirrels are active by day, which is why tree squirrels are out gathering nuts in the morning light.
Nocturnal animals.Eagle: Eagles are diurnal hunters that rely on keen daytime vision, and they roost at night.
Nocturnal animals.Butterfly: Butterflies fly by day, unlike their moth cousins, and they warm up in the sun before they can take off.
Nocturnal animals.Chicken: Chickens are daytime animals, and they get sleepy at dusk and can barely see in the dark.
Nocturnal animals.Bee: Honeybees sleep at night, and the colony's workers go quiet in the hive.
Nocturnal animals.Hawk: Hawks need daylight to hunt by sight and roost after dark, unlike owls.
Nocturnal animals.Chipmunk: Chipmunks are diurnal, scampering about in daylight to stash seeds in cheek pouches.
Nocturnal animals.Meerkat: Meerkats are active by day and bask in the sun on hind legs to warm up after cold desert nights.
Nocturnal animals.Giraffe: Giraffes sleep very little, only about 30 minutes to a few hours, and they're mostly active in daylight.
Nocturnal animals.Gorilla: Gorillas are active by day and build a fresh nest every evening to sleep in.
Nocturnal animals.Hummingbird: Hummingbirds are daytime fliers, though at night they enter torpor, dropping their heart rate dramatically to save energy.
Nocturnal animals.Robin: Robins sing at dawn, but those in cities sometimes sing at night under street lights, which makes them look nocturnal.

British dishes.Fish and chips: Britain's classic takeaway, with early chip shops opened in the 1860s; the dish was never rationed in the Second World War.
British dishes.Shepherd's pie: Made with lamb, as shepherds tend sheep; with beef it's technically a cottage pie, so the name is a clue to the meat.
British dishes.Bangers and mash: Sausages are nicknamed 'bangers' because wartime sausages, packed with water, would burst or pop in the pan.
British dishes.Toad in the hole: Sausages baked in Yorkshire pudding batter; no toad is involved, and the name may come from the way the sausages poke from the batter.
British dishes.Yorkshire pudding: A puffed batter baked in hot fat, which was originally served before the meat to fill diners up.
British dishes.Cornish pasty: It has Protected status; a true pasty is made in Cornwall, with a crimped edge, and tin miners ate them in the pits.
British dishes.Eton mess: A dessert of strawberries, cream and broken meringue, traditionally served at the cricket match at Eton College.
British dishes.Trifle: A layered dessert of sponge, fruit, custard and cream, and one of the oldest in Britain, first named in the 1500s.
British dishes.Bubble and squeak: A fry-up of leftover cabbage and potatoes, named for the noises it makes as it cooks.
British dishes.Scotch egg: A boiled egg wrapped in sausage meat and breadcrumbs; Fortnum & Mason claims to have invented it in 1738.
British dishes.Haggis: Scotland's national dish of sheep offal, onions, oatmeal and spices, traditionally cooked in a stomach and honoured in Burns Night poetry.
British dishes.Welsh rarebit: A savoury cheese sauce on toast, whose name is a joke about Welsh people's supposed love of cheese.
British dishes.Beef Wellington: Fillet of beef wrapped in pastry, which some say was named in honour of the Duke of Wellington, though its history is unclear.
British dishes.Eccles cake: A flaky pastry filled with currants, from the Lancashire town of Eccles, sometimes known as 'squashed fly cake'.
British dishes.Poutine: A Canadian classic from Quebec of chips, cheese curds and gravy, not British.
British dishes.Pierogi: Polish filled dumplings, boiled and then often fried, so not British, though Poland's community in Britain is large.
British dishes.Goulash: A Hungarian stew seasoned with paprika, which began as a herdsmen's meal, so not British.
British dishes.Clam chowder: A New England creamy clam soup, and so American, not British.
British dishes.Gumbo: A thick stew from Louisiana, not British.
British dishes.Jambalaya: A Louisiana rice dish with Creole and Spanish roots, so it is American, not British.
British dishes.Pavlova: A meringue dessert named after the ballerina Anna Pavlova, which both Australia and New Zealand claim.
British dishes.Lamington: A sponge cake coated in chocolate and coconut, an Australian icon rather than a British one.
British dishes.Ratatouille: A French vegetable stew from Provence, made with aubergine, courgette and peppers, so not British.
British dishes.Schnitzel: A breaded cutlet from Austria, not British.

Vegetables that grow underground.Carrot: Carrots grew purple and yellow long before orange; the orange types were bred in the Netherlands in the 1600s, or so the popular story goes.
Vegetables that grow underground.Potato: Potatoes are tubers, stem swellings, not roots; they were domesticated in the Andes and are now the world's fourth biggest food crop.
Vegetables that grow underground.Beet: Beets get their deep red from betalain pigments, which can turn your pee pink in some people, a harmless effect called beeturia.
Vegetables that grow underground.Radish: Radishes are fast growers: some varieties can be picked about three to four weeks after sowing.
Vegetables that grow underground.Turnip: Turnips were a winter staple in Europe, and the original jack-o'-lanterns in Ireland and Scotland were carved from them, not pumpkins.
Vegetables that grow underground.Parsnip: Parsnips were the main sweet starch in Europe before potatoes arrived, and they get sweeter after frost converts starch to sugar.
Vegetables that grow underground.Onion: Onions make you cry because cutting them releases a gas that reacts with your eye's moisture to form a mild irritant.
Vegetables that grow underground.Garlic: Garlic bulbs split into cloves, and China grows around three quarters of the world's supply.
Vegetables that grow underground.Ginger: Ginger is a rhizome, an underground stem, and its heat comes from gingerols, which turn milder and sweeter when cooked.
Vegetables that grow underground.Sweet potato: Sweet potatoes are not closely related to potatoes; they belong to the morning glory family.
Vegetables that grow underground.Rutabaga: Rutabaga is a cross between a cabbage and a turnip; it is called a swede in Britain, after Sweden, where it was first noted.
Vegetables that grow underground.Cassava: Cassava is a staple for hundreds of millions of people, but bitter types contain cyanide compounds, so it must be properly processed.
Vegetables that grow underground.Daikon: Daikon is a giant white radish, whose name means 'big root' in Japanese, and some varieties grow up to a meter long.
Vegetables that grow underground.Broccoli: Broccoli is a flower bud head, a cultivated form of wild cabbage, so you're eating a flower that grows above ground.
Vegetables that grow underground.Cucumber: A cucumber hangs from a vine above ground, and it's botanically a fruit that is about 95 percent water.
Vegetables that grow underground.Zucchini: Zucchini grows above ground on a bushy plant, and it's picked immature; left alone, it can swell into a marrow the size of a baseball bat.
Vegetables that grow underground.Asparagus: Asparagus spears are young shoots poking up out of the ground; left to grow, they become tall, fern-like plants.
Vegetables that grow underground.Artichoke: Artichokes are the flower buds of a thistle, and the edible part is the base of the scales and the heart.
Vegetables that grow underground.Celery: Celery is a stalk, the leaf stem of a plant, that grows up from the ground, rather than a root.
Vegetables that grow underground.Cauliflower: Cauliflower is an above-ground mutation of cabbage, bred for its tight white flower head, though it comes in purple and orange as well.
Vegetables that grow underground.Kale: Kale is a leafy cabbage relative that grows above ground, and cold weather turns its starches into sugars, making it sweeter.
Vegetables that grow underground.Eggplant: Eggplants are berries botanically and hang on bushy plants, and they were once white and egg-shaped, which explains the name.
Vegetables that grow underground.Okra: Okra is the immature seed pod of a plant related to hibiscus, and it grows up above ground.
Vegetables that grow underground.Bell pepper: A bell pepper is a fruit that grows above ground, and the red, yellow and orange ones are just riper stages of the green.

Things made from rice.Sake: Japanese brewed drink made by fermenting polished rice with koji mold. Unlike wine, it is brewed, closer to beer, but strong.
Things made from rice.Mochi: Glutinous rice steamed and pounded into stretchy dough. Pounding it with giant mallets is a Japanese New Year ritual.
Things made from rice.Risotto: Italian dish of short-grain rice stirred slowly so it releases starch and turns creamy. Arborio and carnaroli are the classic varieties.
Things made from rice.Rice paper: Translucent Vietnamese wrappers made from rice flour and water, dried in sheets and softened in water for fresh spring rolls.
Things made from rice.Jambalaya: A Louisiana one-pot rice dish related to Spanish paella. The rice cooks right in the spiced stock with sausage and seafood.
Things made from rice.Arancini: Sicilian fried rice balls whose name means little oranges. They are stuffed with ragu, peas or cheese.
Things made from rice.Congee: Rice simmered until it dissolves into porridge, a breakfast and comfort food across Asia, often topped with pickles, eggs or fish.
Things made from rice.Rice vinegar: Made by fermenting rice into alcohol and then into acid. It seasons sushi rice and is milder and sweeter than most vinegars.
Things made from rice.Onigiri: Japanese rice balls, often wrapped in nori, with a filling like pickled plum or salmon. They are a classic lunchbox and convenience store snack.
Things made from rice.Paella: The pan itself gave the dish its name, and the best part is the crispy bottom layer of rice, called socarrat.
Things made from rice.Biryani: Layered rice and spiced meat sealed and steamed in its own juices. Hyderabad and Lucknow each claim their own famous version.
Things made from rice.Rice Krispies: Puffed rice cereal known for its snap, crackle and pop. Its mascot elves have been talking on the box since the 1930s.
Things made from rice.Couscous: Actually tiny pasta made from semolina wheat, not a grain, so it does not belong with rice despite the similar look.
Things made from rice.Quinoa: A seed from the Andes, not a cereal at all. Incas called it the mother grain and held it sacred.
Things made from rice.Polenta: Cornmeal porridge from northern Italy. Corn arrived from the Americas, so polenta was once made from other grains like millet or spelt.
Things made from rice.Bulgur: Cracked parboiled wheat. It is the cousin of couscous and the main ingredient of tabbouleh.
Things made from rice.Orzo: Italian for barley, but orzo pasta is actually made from wheat. It only looks like grains of rice.
Things made from rice.Tapioca pearls: Chewy balls made from cassava starch, the bubbles in bubble tea. Cassava is a root, not a grain.
Things made from rice.Pearl barley: Barley with its husk and bran polished away. It is the classic thickener of Scotch broth and cooked rice-like.
Things made from rice.Semolina: Granular flour from durum wheat. It is the basis of most dried Italian pasta.
Things made from rice.Farro: An ancient wheat variety, sometimes called emmer, that Roman legionnaires carried as rations. It cooks nutty and chewy.
Things made from rice.Gnocchi: Italian dumplings that are usually made with potato and wheat flour. Their name may come from the Italian word for knot.
Things made from rice.Grits: Coarsely ground corn simmered into a creamy porridge. They are a fixture of the American South.
Things made from rice.Tabbouleh: A Levantine salad built on parsley, with bulgur wheat as a minor ingredient. Traditionally it is more green than grain.

Rum cocktails.Mojito: Muddled mint, lime, sugar, soda, and white rum. Cuba's most famous drink, and legend ties it to sailors seeking a remedy under Sir Francis Drake.
Rum cocktails.Daiquiri: Rum, lime juice, and sugar, named for a Cuban mining town. Only three ingredients; naval officers helped spread it in the early 1900s.
Rum cocktails.Piña colada: Rum, pineapple, and cream of coconut. Puerto Rico made it its official drink in 1978; two bartenders there each claim to have invented it.
Rum cocktails.Mai tai: Rum, lime, orgeat, and curaçao. Trader Vic claimed it, and 'Maita'i' is Tahitian for 'good', supposedly what a guest exclaimed on tasting it.
Rum cocktails.Dark 'n' Stormy: Bermuda's national drink, with a specific brand of dark rum and ginger beer. The brand has trademarked the drink's name.
Rum cocktails.Cuba libre: Rum and cola with lime, meaning 'free Cuba'. Said to have begun in Havana after the Spanish-American War, around 1900.
Rum cocktails.Zombie: Created by Don the Beachcomber in 1934 with several rums; strong enough that bars limit guests to two.
Rum cocktails.Hurricane: New Orleans' rum drink with passion fruit, served in a hurricane-lamp shaped glass. It began as a way to use up surplus rum.
Rum cocktails.Painkiller: A creamy rum drink with pineapple, orange, and coconut from the British Virgin Islands; the name tells of what it does to sore heads.
Rum cocktails.Planter's punch: A rum punch from Barbados and Jamaica, remembered by a rhyme: one of sour, two of sweet, three of strong, four of weak.
Rum cocktails.El Presidente: A Cuban classic of rum, vermouth, curaçao, and grenadine. It was named for a Cuban president, in 1920s Havana.
Rum cocktails.Margarita: A trap: tequila, lime, and triple sec, not rum. Don't confuse it with the daiquiri, its rum cousin.
Rum cocktails.Paloma: A trap: tequila and grapefruit soda make Mexico's favourite highball, more popular there than the Margarita. No rum anywhere in it.
Rum cocktails.Negroni: A trap: it is gin, Campari, and sweet vermouth in equal parts, a bitter Italian aperitif. Rum has no place in it.
Rum cocktails.Martini: Gin or vodka with dry vermouth, shaken or stirred; James Bond ordered his shaken. Not rum.
Rum cocktails.Cosmopolitan: A trap: vodka is the base here, with triple sec, cranberry, and lime. It looks tropical and fruity, but there is no rum in it.
Rum cocktails.Moscow mule: Vodka and ginger beer in a copper mug. It is vodka-based, though it sounds like a cousin of Dark 'n' Stormy.
Rum cocktails.Old Fashioned: A trap: whiskey, bitters, sugar, and a twist make this one, though a rum Old Fashioned exists as a variation. The classic is whiskey.
Rum cocktails.Manhattan: Rye or bourbon with sweet vermouth, said to be created in Manhattan for a banquet in 1870s. It uses whiskey.
Rum cocktails.Sidecar: A trap: cognac, orange liqueur, and lemon juice, usually with a sugared rim. It is a brandy classic, not a rum drink.
Rum cocktails.Whiskey sour: A trap: despite sharing a sour's lime-or-lemon template with the Daiquiri, this one is built on bourbon or rye, not rum.
Rum cocktails.Bloody Mary: Vodka and tomato juice. Not rum, but named after Queen Mary I, the Bloody Mary of English history.
Rum cocktails.Aperol spritz: Prosecco, Aperol, and soda. The Italian aperitif has no rum, and in Italy it now outsells many classics.

Seas around Europe.Aegean: The sea of Greek islands is named after King Aegeus of Athens, who in legend leapt into it.

Seas around Europe.Irish Sea: The sea between Britain and Ireland is shallow and includes the Isle of Man.
Seas around Europe.Tyrrhenian: West of Italy, this Mediterranean sea is named for the Etruscans, whom the Greeks called Tyrrhenoi.
Seas around Europe.Ionian: Between Greece and southern Italy, it holds the Calypso Deep, the deepest point of the Mediterranean.
Seas around Europe.Norwegian Sea: The Gulf Stream warms it, keeping Norway's coast ice-free far north of the Arctic Circle.
Seas around Europe.Ligurian: This part of the Mediterranean touches Genoa and the Italian and French Riviera.
Seas around Europe.Barents: Named for Dutch explorer Willem Barentsz, this Arctic sea lies north of Norway and Russia.
Seas around Europe.Red Sea: This sea between Africa and Asia is famous for coral reefs, but it is not a European sea.
Seas around Europe.Caribbean: Its waters border Central and South America, and it is far from Europe.
Seas around Europe.Arabian Sea: This northwest part of the Indian Ocean lies between India and Arabia.
Seas around Europe.South China Sea: A huge sea in Southeast Asia, whose ownership of the islands is disputed between several nations.
Seas around Europe.Coral Sea: It borders Australia's Great Barrier Reef, and it was the site of a major 1942 naval battle.
Seas around Europe.Yellow Sea: It is named for the yellow sediment from Chinese rivers, and it lies between China and Korea.
Seas around Europe.Bering Sea: Between Alaska and Russia, it is named for Vitus Bering, a Danish explorer.

Seas around Europe.Java Sea: This shallow sea lies between Borneo and Java in Indonesia.
Seas around Europe.Andaman Sea: This part of the Indian Ocean lies off Myanmar and Thailand.
Seas around Europe.Sargasso Sea: The only sea with no coastline, bounded instead by ocean currents, it is named for floating sargassum seaweed.
Seas around Europe.Timor Sea: It lies between Australia and Timor, far from Europe.

Places in Vietnam.Phu Quoc: Vietnam's biggest island lies close to Cambodia, and it is renowned for its fish sauce and pepper.
Places in Vietnam.Dalat: A cool highland city founded by the French as a retreat, and it is called the City of Eternal Spring.
Places in Vietnam.Siem Reap: The town beside Angkor Wat is in Cambodia, the neighbor that lies to Vietnam's southwest.
Places in Vietnam.Phnom Penh: Cambodia's capital, a few hours by road from Ho Chi Minh City, is where the Mekong River splits into several channels.
Places in Vietnam.Vientiane: The capital of Laos is on the Mekong, and it is one of Asia's quietest capitals.
Places in Vietnam.Luang Prabang: A Laotian royal capital with golden temples, famous for the dawn alms procession of monks.

Places in Vietnam.Kuala Lumpur: Malaysia's capital, whose Petronas Towers were the tallest buildings in the world from 1998 to 2004.
Places in Vietnam.Angkor Wat: The largest religious monument in the world is in Cambodia, and its image appears on the Cambodian flag.
Places in Vietnam.Yangon: Myanmar's biggest city has the glittering Shwedagon Pagoda, and it lies to Vietnam's west.
Places in Vietnam.Guangzhou: A big southern Chinese city once known as Canton, which lies north of Vietnam but is not in it.
Places in Vietnam.Macau: A former Portuguese colony on China's coast, now a gambling hub, and not in Vietnam.

Elements you could safely hold in your h.Silver: The best electrical conductor of all metals, and it naturally fights bacteria.
Elements you could safely hold in your h.Copper: Copper surfaces kill many bacteria within hours, which is why some hospitals use copper door handles.
Elements you could safely hold in your h.Iron: It is in your blood, where each haemoglobin molecule carries oxygen using iron.
Elements you could safely hold in your h.Aluminum: Once rarer than gold, since it was hard to extract; Napoleon III reportedly served honoured guests on aluminium plates.
Elements you could safely hold in your h.Tin: Bending a bar of tin makes an audible 'cry' as its crystals shift.
Elements you could safely hold in your h.Zinc: Modern US pennies are mostly zinc with a thin copper coat.
Elements you could safely hold in your h.Platinum: Rarer than gold in Earth's crust, and a hand can hold a piece safely.
Elements you could safely hold in your h.Titanium: As strong as steel but about 45% lighter, it is safe to touch and used in implants.
Elements you could safely hold in your h.Silicon: Safe to hold, and as the base of computer chips it makes up much of what sand is.
Elements you could safely hold in your h.Tungsten: It has the highest melting point of any metal, around 3,400 degrees Celsius, and a lump is perfectly safe to hold, though very heavy.
Elements you could safely hold in your h.Sodium: It bursts into flame on water, so it is kept under oil.
Elements you could safely hold in your h.Potassium: Even more fierce than sodium in water, burning with a lilac flame.
Elements you could safely hold in your h.Cesium: It melts at about 28 degrees Celsius, so it would liquefy in your hand, and it explodes in water.
Elements you could safely hold in your h.Mercury: The only common metal that is liquid at room temperature, and its vapour is toxic.
Elements you could safely hold in your h.Plutonium: Radioactive and toxic, yet plutonium-238 has powered Voyager and Mars rovers.
Elements you could safely hold in your h.Polonium: Marie Curie named it after Poland; it is intensely radioactive and was used to poison Alexander Litvinenko in 2006.
Elements you could safely hold in your h.Fluorine: The most reactive element, a pale gas that attacks almost anything, even glass.
Elements you could safely hold in your h.Chlorine: A poison gas in the First World War, but in small amounts it disinfects pools and drinking water.
Elements you could safely hold in your h.Radium: Radioactive and glows faintly blue; Marie Curie's notebooks are still radioactive.
Elements you could safely hold in your h.Francium: The rarest natural element, with less than about 30 grams in the whole crust at any time.
Elements you could safely hold in your h.Rubidium: A soft metal that ignites in air and is used in atomic clocks.
Elements you could safely hold in your h.White phosphorus: It ignites spontaneously in air, so it is stored under water, and it causes severe burns.
Elements you could safely hold in your h.Bromine: One of only two elements liquid at room temperature, with red-brown fumes; the name means 'stench'.

Invisible to the naked eye.Ultraviolet light: Your eyes see only a thin slice of light. UV is just beyond violet, though bees see it and flowers show hidden UV patterns.
Invisible to the naked eye.Infrared: Infrared is felt as heat, not seen. Snakes like pit vipers sense it to hunt warm prey in total darkness.
Invisible to the naked eye.Radio waves: Radio waves can be longer than a football field, and carry everything from FM music to signals from distant galaxies.
Invisible to the naked eye.X-rays: X-rays were found by accident in 1895 by Wilhelm Röntgen, who soon X-rayed his wife's hand, ring and all.
Invisible to the naked eye.Oxygen gas: Air is about 21 percent oxygen, yet it is totally colorless and invisible, so you cannot see what you breathe.
Invisible to the naked eye.Carbon dioxide: Carbon dioxide is invisible, but it is what bubbles in soda and what plants pull from the air to build themselves.
Invisible to the naked eye.Atoms: Atoms are so small that millions would fit across a hair's width, yet nearly all of each atom is empty space.
Invisible to the naked eye.Viruses: Most viruses are far too small for light microscopes. Billions can float in a single drop of seawater.
Invisible to the naked eye.Bacteria: A single bacterium is invisible, but a colony of millions becomes the visible film on your teeth or on an agar plate.
Invisible to the naked eye.Wi-Fi signals: Wi-Fi uses radio waves at about 2.4 or 5 GHz, the same family as microwaves. You can't see them, but your phone does.
Invisible to the naked eye.Microwaves: Microwaves are invisible radio waves. The oven's waves jiggle water molecules, so food heats while the plate stays cooler.
Invisible to the naked eye.Rainbow: A rainbow is plainly visible, but it is not a physical object. Each viewer sees their own, made by sunlight in raindrops.
Invisible to the naked eye.Lightning: Lightning is bright enough to see from miles away, and its flash is hotter than the Sun's surface.
Invisible to the naked eye.Aurora: Auroras are visible glows high up in the sky, as solar particles strike air molecules about 100 km up.
Invisible to the naked eye.Smoke: Smoke is visible because tiny particles scatter light. Its color shows what's burning, from white to black.
Invisible to the naked eye.Fog: Fog is just a cloud at ground level. Its water droplets scatter light, so you see a white wall rather than far away.
Invisible to the naked eye.The Moon: The Moon is visible even in daytime, and its surface is dark, reflecting only about 12 percent of sunlight.
Invisible to the naked eye.Venus: Venus is the brightest planet and has been spotted in daylight. Its thick clouds reflect most of the sunlight hitting them.
Invisible to the naked eye.Flea: A flea is about 2 to 3 mm, small but visible. It can jump over 100 times its own body length.
Invisible to the naked eye.Grain of salt: A grain of salt is visible, around 0.3 mm across. Look closely and you can see its tiny cube shape.
Invisible to the naked eye.Human hair: A human hair is about 70 micrometers wide. That is thin, but it is still visible, especially against a plain background.
Invisible to the naked eye.Andromeda Galaxy: Andromeda is the farthest thing most people can see unaided, about 2.5 million light-years away, from a dark site.
Invisible to the naked eye.ISS: The ISS is visible as a moving bright star, as sunlight reflects off its panels, and it circles Earth every 90 minutes.
Invisible to the naked eye.Ant: An ant is visible, though tiny. Yet an ant can carry things many times its own weight.
