K-pop groups.Twice: The nine-member group formed through the 2015 TV show "Sixteen", with members from Korea, Japan and Taiwan.
K-pop groups.EXO: It debuted in 2012 with twelve members in two sub-groups, EXO-K and EXO-M, which released songs in Korean and Mandarin.
K-pop groups.Big Bang: The five-member YG group, formed in 2006, helped export K-pop abroad, and G-Dragon is its best-known member.
K-pop groups.Stray Kids: Created through a reality show, the self-producing group became the first act to debut at No. 1 on the Billboard 200 with five albums in a row.
K-pop groups.NewJeans: It debuted in 2022, and its five teenage members are known for a Y2K retro sound in songs like "Hype Boy".
K-pop groups.Seventeen: The 13-member group is named after its members and units, and it writes and choreographs much of its own work.
K-pop groups.Red Velvet: The group's name reflects its dual concept, red for catchy pop and velvet for smooth R&B.
K-pop groups.Girls' Generation: Formed in 2007, this nine-member group's "Gee" topped Korean charts for weeks, and it is known as SNSD.
K-pop groups.Aespa: The group pairs four human members with virtual avatars, a concept built around the idea of meeting your digital self.
K-pop groups.Super Junior: It formed in 2005 as a huge rotating group that grew to 13 members, and it started the Hallyu wave across Asia.
K-pop groups.Arashi: It is a Japanese boy band from the agency Johnny's, not K-pop, and its name means "storm".
K-pop groups.AKB48: It is a Japanese idol group named after Akihabara, Tokyo's electronics district, with dozens of rotating members.
K-pop groups.Perfume: This three-member Japanese electropop group is from Hiroshima, and its stage shows use striking tech and visuals.
K-pop groups.One Direction: The British-Irish band formed on "The X Factor" in 2010 and sold more than 70 million records.
K-pop groups.Little Mix: The first group to win "The X Factor" UK, in 2011, they are British, and have scored multiple UK number ones.
K-pop groups.Westlife: This Irish pop group had 14 UK number-one singles, though it is no K-pop act.
K-pop groups.Spice Girls: This 1990s British girl group sold over 100 million records, and its slogan was "Girl Power".
K-pop groups.Backstreet Boys: The Orlando group, formed in 1993, is one of the best-selling boy bands ever, though its sound is American pop.
K-pop groups.Babymetal: This Japanese group mixes idol pop with heavy metal, a twist that made them famous worldwide.
K-pop groups.SMAP: A Japanese boy band that split in 2016, with a farewell single "Sekai ni Hitotsu dake no Hana" among the best-selling in Japan.
K-pop groups.Morning Musume: It formed in 1997 as a Japanese idol group in which members "graduate" and are replaced by newcomers.
K-pop groups.Jonas Brothers: The three siblings from New Jersey rose through Disney Channel, and they are American, not Korean.

Woodworking tools.Chisel: Woodworkers pare joints with it, and it's among the oldest tools around, with versions found in prehistoric sites.
Woodworking tools.Lathe: A spinning workpiece meets a fixed cutting tool, and the lathe is old enough that Egyptians turned wood this way thousands of years ago.
Woodworking tools.Router: Spinning at about 20,000 rpm, a router's bit hollows grooves and shapes decorative edges in wood.
Woodworking tools.Jigsaw: Its narrow blade moves up and down to cut curves. The puzzle takes its name from the saw, since early ones were cut with it.
Woodworking tools.Hand plane: Pushed along a board, it shaves off thin curls, and a sharp one leaves a finish smoother than most sandpaper.
Woodworking tools.Mallet: A wooden hammer taps chisels without damaging their handles, and it's got a broad head that spreads the blow.
Woodworking tools.Clamp: A woodworker's rule of thumb says you can never own enough of them, because glue-ups need pressure while the joint dries.
Woodworking tools.Sandpaper: It's a toolbox staple, though it's not actually sand. Its grit is usually garnet, aluminum oxide or silicon carbide on paper.
Woodworking tools.Bandsaw: An endless loop of toothed steel runs over two wheels, which lets it saw curves and also resaw thick boards into thin veneers.
Woodworking tools.Spokeshave: Wheelwrights used this two-handled blade to shape spokes, and chairmakers still use it for smoothing curved parts.
Woodworking tools.Wood glue: A well-made glue joint is stronger than the wood around it, so the board often breaks before the joint does.
Woodworking tools.Miter saw: It swings to cut precise angles, most often the 45-degree corners for picture frames and trim.
Woodworking tools.Crochet hook: Yarn crafters pull loops with this one hooked tool, but a woodshop has no use for it.
Woodworking tools.Knitting needle: Needles come from the yarn world, and while some are of wood they're for stitches, not for shaping timber.
Woodworking tools.Kiln: Potters fire clay with it, though woodworkers use a kiln too, to dry lumber, and the one here belongs to ceramics.
Woodworking tools.Easel: This stand holds a painter's canvas upright, so it's an art supply, not a shop tool.
Woodworking tools.Thimble: A small cap on a sewer's finger shields it from the needle. Thimbles date back thousands of years.
Woodworking tools.Bobbin: This spool holds thread in a sewing machine or in lacemaking, and lace is sometimes called bobbin lace.
Woodworking tools.Pinking shears: Their zigzag blades stop fabric edges from fraying, and the name comes from the old word pinking for cutting a scalloped edge.
Woodworking tools.Tripod: Photographers steady their cameras on three legs, and a woodworker would not call it a shop tool.
Woodworking tools.Soldering iron: It melts metal to join wires and electronics, not wood, though it's got a use in pyrography, burning designs into timber.
Woodworking tools.Loom: Weavers use this frame to interlace threads into cloth. It's among the oldest human machines, and not a shop tool.
Woodworking tools.Palette knife: Painters use the flat blade to spread thick paint, and cooks use a similar one for icing. It isn't for wood.
Woodworking tools.Pipette: Laboratories use this slim tube to move precise small amounts of liquid, so it's far from a workshop tool.

Sports played with a stick.Ice hockey: Players slap a hard rubber puck with the stick, and a hard shot can top 160 km/h.
Sports played with a stick.Field hockey: Sticks have a flat face on one side only, and a player who hits with the round side is penalized.
Sports played with a stick.Lacrosse: Indigenous peoples played this game for centuries, and some matches ran over several days and involved hundreds of players.
Sports played with a stick.Hurling: Ireland's ancient game uses a flat-bladed hurley and a leather ball, and it's claimed to be among the fastest field sports.
Sports played with a stick.Bandy: An old cousin of ice hockey played on a soccer-pitch-sized ice field with a ball. It's big in Russia and Sweden.
Sports played with a stick.Floorball: This indoor hockey-like sport uses lightweight sticks and a plastic ball with holes, and it began in Sweden in the 1970s.
Sports played with a stick.Shinty: Scotland's Highland game is related to hurling, and it's played with a stick called a caman and a leather-covered ball.
Sports played with a stick.Ringette: Invented in Canada in the 1960s, it's played on ice with a straight stick and a rubber ring, and it's mostly played by girls and women.
Sports played with a stick.Camogie: This Irish stick game is a women's version of hurling, played with a slightly lighter stick and organized since 1904.
Sports played with a stick.Baseball: Hitters use a bat, not a stick, and the difference matters when sports are sorted by equipment.
Sports played with a stick.Cricket: Players use a bat, a wide flat willow blade, so it falls outside the stick sports.
Sports played with a stick.Kabaddi: Raiders hold their breath and chant as they tag opponents, and the sport needs no equipment at all.
Sports played with a stick.Croquet: It uses mallets to strike balls through hoops, which makes it a mallet game and not a stick sport.
Sports played with a stick.Tennis: It's played with racquets, and the strings are tuned to the player's style.
Sports played with a stick.Badminton: Racquets hit a feathered shuttlecock, and it can top 400 km/h, the fastest of racquet sports.
Sports played with a stick.Squash: A hollow rubber ball in a four-wall court gets hit with a racquet, which isn't a stick.
Sports played with a stick.Fencing: Fencers use blades, a foil, epee or sabre, rather than sticks.
Sports played with a stick.Volleyball: Hands, not sticks, strike the ball across a net, and the game was invented in 1895 as a gentler alternative to basketball.
Sports played with a stick.Handball: The ball is thrown and no stick is needed. It's played with hands only.
Sports played with a stick.Water polo: Swimmers use hands to throw a ball, so it's a stickless sport, and there's no treading the bottom.
Sports played with a stick.Basketball: The game was invented in 1891 with peach baskets, and it uses hands and no stick.
Sports played with a stick.Rugby: Players carry and kick an oval ball, and no stick is used.
Sports played with a stick.Soccer: Players use their feet, not sticks, and the world's most popular sport needs just a ball.
Sports played with a stick.Netball: Players can't run with the ball, and they pass it by hand toward a hoop, so no stick is involved. It grew out of early basketball.

Sports invented in Great Britain.Soccer: The rules were codified in 1863 when London's Football Association formed. Soccer is a shortening of Association.
Sports invented in Great Britain.Rugby: Named after Rugby School. The tale that William Webb Ellis picked up the ball in 1823 is probably a myth.
Sports invented in Great Britain.Cricket: A Test match can last five days and still end in a draw. The first official Test was played in 1877.
Sports invented in Great Britain.Squash: Born at Harrow School in the 19th century and named for the way the soft ball squashes when hit.
Sports invented in Great Britain.Table tennis: Began as a Victorian after-dinner pastime, with ping-pong as its sound. Olympic since 1988.
Sports invented in Great Britain.Golf: Played at St Andrews since the 1400s. Scotland banned it in 1457 because it distracted men from archery practice.
Sports invented in Great Britain.Curling: Scottish: the oldest known stone, dated 1511, was found near Dunblane.
Sports invented in Great Britain.Netball: Grew from early women's basketball in 1890s England. No dribbling is allowed, and a player can't move while holding the ball.
Sports invented in Great Britain.Rounders: A bat-and-ball game played in England since Tudor times. Some historians say baseball descends from it.
Sports invented in Great Britain.Basketball: Invented by James Naismith, a Canadian, in Massachusetts in 1891.
Sports invented in Great Britain.Volleyball: Invented in 1895 in Holyoke, Massachusetts, not Britain.
Sports invented in Great Britain.Baseball: American, though it evolved partly from rounders. The Abner Doubleday origin story is a myth.
Sports invented in Great Britain.American football: It developed from rugby and soccer on US college campuses.
Sports invented in Great Britain.Ice hockey: Canadian, with early organised games in Montreal in 1875.
Sports invented in Great Britain.Judo: Japanese, founded by Jigoro Kano in 1882.
Sports invented in Great Britain.Karate: It's from Okinawa in Japan, where it grew from local and Chinese fighting arts.
Sports invented in Great Britain.Taekwondo: Korean in origin, and the name means the way of the foot and fist.
Sports invented in Great Britain.Lacrosse: Based on Native American stickball, and Canada's national summer sport.
Sports invented in Great Britain.Pickleball: Invented in 1965 on Bainbridge Island, Washington.
Sports invented in Great Britain.Sumo: Japan's ancient wrestling, over 1,500 years old.
Sports invented in Great Britain.Jai alai: A Basque game from Spain, with the ball reaching speeds over 150 mph.
Sports invented in Great Britain.Hurling: Irish, not British. The Gaelic Athletic Association that governs it was formed in 1884.
Sports invented in Great Britain.Gaelic football: Irish, not British, and played under the GAA, which was founded in 1884.
Sports invented in Great Britain.Handball: Modern team handball was formalised in Germany and Scandinavia around 1900.

Circus skills.Juggling: Juggling appears in Egyptian tomb art about 4,000 years old. A famous result: three balls can be juggled in more patterns than most people guess.
Circus skills.Trapeze: The flying trapeze was devised by Frenchman Jules Léotard in the 1850s. His close-fitting outfit, the leotard, bears his name.
Circus skills.Tightrope walking: Philippe Petit walked a wire between the Twin Towers in 1974, over 400 meters up. Walkers use long poles to keep their balance.
Circus skills.Unicycling: Unicyclists ride on a single wheel with no freewheel; the pedals turn the wheel directly. Some even play hockey or climb mountains this way.
Circus skills.Stilt walking: Circus stilt walkers can tower several meters tall. Shepherds in southwestern France once used stilts to see over marshland.
Circus skills.Fire breathing: Fire breathers don't swallow flame; they spray a fine mist of fuel through a flame, and the mouth must be kept moving to avoid burns. It's very risky.
Circus skills.Aerial silks: Performers climb and drop while wrapped in two long fabric panels hanging from a rig. It demands tremendous grip and core strength.
Circus skills.Clowning: Joseph Grimaldi, who died in 1837, was so famous in London that clowns are still nicknamed 'Joeys' after him.
Circus skills.Contortion: Contortionists have unusually flexible spines and joints, but years of training matter more. Many start as small children.
Circus skills.Plate spinning: The performer sets plates spinning on thin poles and rushes between them, returning just as each starts to wobble.
Circus skills.Acrobatics: The word comes from Greek for 'walking on tiptoe'. Circus acrobats often form human pyramids, with the strongest as the base.
Circus skills.Knitting: Knitting is a craft done at home, not a circus skill. It likely dates to Egypt around the 11th century, in the form of knitted socks.
Circus skills.Pottery: Pottery is among the oldest crafts, with clay vessels more than 15,000 years old. It's studio work, not a big top act.
Circus skills.Birdwatching: Watching birds is a quiet pastime that has produced citizen science records covering millions of sightings. No tent required.
Circus skills.Chess: Chess is a board game, not a circus act, though it's sometimes played live with people as pieces. Computers have beaten champions since 1997.
Circus skills.Golf: Golf is a field sport, not a circus skill. The sport's most famous rule of thumb: the lowest score wins.
Circus skills.Fishing: Fishing is a patient hobby, not a performance skill. Sometimes a hobby doesn't need an audience.
Circus skills.Bowling: Bowling is a lane sport. A perfect game is 12 strikes in a row for 300 points, but you won't see it in a circus ring.
Circus skills.Sudoku: Sudoku is a number puzzle popularized in Japan, and it is for sitting down quietly, not for performing under a big top.
Circus skills.Gardening: Gardening is a slow hobby with no stage required, and it may lower stress levels measurably, studies suggest.
Circus skills.Quilting: Quilting stitches layers of fabric into patterns; it is a craft practiced in quiet homes, not an act you'd see in a ring.
Circus skills.Stamp collecting: Stamp collecting, or philately, is quiet and absorbing. The British Penny Black from 1840 was the world's first adhesive stamp.
Circus skills.Rowing: Rowing is a boat sport; rowers face backward as they pull. It's not a circus discipline.
Circus skills.Bridge: Bridge is a card game, not a circus skill. It's a trick-taking partnership game that hundreds of millions play worldwide.

Nintendo consoles and handhelds.NES: The Nintendo Entertainment System arrived in the US in 1985 and helped revive the games industry after the 1983 crash. It's the Western Famicom.
Nintendo consoles and handhelds.SNES: The Super NES launched in Japan in 1990 as the Super Famicom, and Super Mario World was its star launch title.
Nintendo consoles and handhelds.N64: The Nintendo 64, 1996, used cartridges rather than discs and introduced the analog stick on a three-pronged controller.
Nintendo consoles and handhelds.GameCube: Launched in 2001, the compact purple GameCube played small mini discs. Its handle on top made it easy to carry.
Nintendo consoles and handhelds.Wii: The Wii of 2006 used motion controls and sold over 100 million units, bringing in many non-gamers.
Nintendo consoles and handhelds.Wii U: The Wii U, launched in 2012, had a tablet controller. It sold poorly, but its successor, the Switch, borrowed ideas from it.
Nintendo consoles and handhelds.Switch: The Switch launched in 2017 as a hybrid that plays at home or on the go, and it became Nintendo's best-selling hardware line.
Nintendo consoles and handhelds.Game Boy: Nintendo's 1989 handheld was designed by Gunpei Yokoi. Its grayish-green screen and Tetris bundle helped it sell tens of millions.
Nintendo consoles and handhelds.Game Boy Advance: The 2001 Game Boy Advance upgraded the line to 32-bit. It played original Game Boy titles too.
Nintendo consoles and handhelds.DS: The Nintendo DS, from 2004, had two screens and a touch screen, and it ranks among the best-selling consoles ever.
Nintendo consoles and handhelds.3DS: The 3DS from 2011 could show 3D without glasses, though many players switched the effect off.
Nintendo consoles and handhelds.Virtual Boy: Released in 1995, this red-and-black stereoscopic console was a flop that lasted only about a year in stores. Yokoi designed it.
Nintendo consoles and handhelds.Game & Watch: Starting in 1980, these single-game LCD handhelds also had a clock. They anticipated the Game Boy and were designed by Gunpei Yokoi.
Nintendo consoles and handhelds.Genesis: Genesis is a Sega console, a rival to Nintendo, so it doesn't belong here.
Nintendo consoles and handhelds.Dreamcast: Sega's last console, ended in 2001, and is not a Nintendo product.
Nintendo consoles and handhelds.Saturn: The Saturn was Sega's, going against Sony's PlayStation, not Nintendo's.
Nintendo consoles and handhelds.PlayStation: The PlayStation is Sony's, though it began as a Nintendo CD add-on project that fell through.
Nintendo consoles and handhelds.Xbox: Xbox is Microsoft's console; it entered the market in 2001 against Nintendo and Sony.
Nintendo consoles and handhelds.PSP: Sony's PlayStation Portable arrived in 2004 to challenge the DS, and it is not by Nintendo.
Nintendo consoles and handhelds.Game Gear: Game Gear was Sega's color handheld that challenged the Game Boy, so it's not from Nintendo.
Nintendo consoles and handhelds.Atari 2600: Atari's 1977 console made home gaming mainstream, and the maker was Atari, not Nintendo.
Nintendo consoles and handhelds.Steam Deck: Valve's handheld PC launched in 2022 and can play a huge PC library; it's not Nintendo's.
Nintendo consoles and handhelds.Neo Geo: SNK's Neo Geo of 1990 offered arcade games at home, but at a high price. It isn't Nintendo.
Nintendo consoles and handhelds.Ouya: Ouya was a small Android console funded on Kickstarter in 2012, and it's not by Nintendo.

Royal houses of Europe.Tudor: Henry VII seized the crown at Bosworth in 1485. The dynasty ended with Elizabeth I in 1603, who left no children.
Royal houses of Europe.Stuart: Scotland's royal house inherited England's throne in 1603, then lost it in civil war when Charles I was beheaded in 1649.
Royal houses of Europe.Windsor: This name was adopted in 1917, when George V dropped the German-sounding Saxe-Coburg and Gotha in the middle of World War I.
Royal houses of Europe.Habsburg: They ruled Austria for over six centuries and, at their peak, much of Europe and Spain's empire, with a famously prominent jaw.
Royal houses of Europe.Romanov: Russia's last dynasty ruled from 1613 until Nicholas II abdicated in 1917. The family was executed the following year.
Royal houses of Europe.Bourbon: A French dynasty that also ruled Spain, where King Felipe VI is still a Bourbon. Kentucky's Bourbon County took its name from them.
Royal houses of Europe.Plantagenet: The name probably comes from the broom sprig, planta genista, an ancestor wore. They ruled England from 1154 to 1485.
Royal houses of Europe.Hanover: A German house whose George I became British king in 1714, because Parliament barred Catholic heirs with a closer claim.
Royal houses of Europe.York: Its badge was the white rose. It fought the Lancastrians in the Wars of the Roses, and Richard III was its last king.
Royal houses of Europe.Lancaster: The red-rose side of the Wars of the Roses. Henry IV, V and VI were all Lancastrian kings of England.
Royal houses of Europe.Valois: Ruled France from 1328 to 1589. Edward III of England's rival claim to their throne helped spark the Hundred Years' War.
Royal houses of Europe.Hohenzollern: Rulers of Prussia and, from 1871, the German Empire. Wilhelm II, the last emperor, abdicated in 1918.
Royal houses of Europe.Capet: Founded by Hugh Capet in 987. Louis XVI was guillotined in 1793 under the humbling name Citizen Louis Capet.
Royal houses of Europe.Ming: A Chinese dynasty (1368 to 1644) famed for blue-and-white porcelain and the Forbidden City. It reigned in Asia, not Europe.
Royal houses of Europe.Tang: China's golden age of poetry and Silk Road trade, 618 to 907. A dynasty of Asia, not a European house.
Royal houses of Europe.Qing: China's last dynasty ended in 1912 when the child emperor Puyi abdicated. Not a European house.
Royal houses of Europe.Han: Its long rule from 206 BC to AD 220 gave China's majority ethnic group its name. Chinese, not European.
Royal houses of Europe.Tokugawa: Japan's shogun family kept the peace for about 250 years until 1868. A powerful Asian house, not a European one.
Royal houses of Europe.Mughal: This Indian dynasty built the Taj Mahal. Its emperors were descendants of Timur and Genghis Khan, not European royals.
Royal houses of Europe.Abbasid: These caliphs ruled from Baghdad, where the House of Wisdom flourished. It was an Islamic dynasty, not a European one.
Royal houses of Europe.Joseon: Korea's dynasty lasted over 500 years, from 1392. Under it the Korean alphabet, Hangul, was created. Not European.
Royal houses of Europe.Shang: China's earliest dynasty with written records, which survive as oracle bones. An Asian dynasty, not a European house.
Royal houses of Europe.Song: Chinese dynasty that used paper money and gunpowder weapons centuries before Europe. It ruled in Asia.
Royal houses of Europe.Ashikaga: A Japanese shogun family of the Muromachi period, in power from the 1330s to 1573. Not European royalty.

Things that are flammable.Paper: Paper ignites around 450 degrees Fahrenheit, which is where Ray Bradbury got the title Fahrenheit 451.
Things that are flammable.Matches: Safety matches only light on the special strip on the box, because red phosphorus and the head chemicals must meet.
Things that are flammable.Gasoline: It is the vapor, not the liquid, that burns; gasoline gives off ignitable fumes even at well below freezing.
Things that are flammable.Cotton wool: Cotton wool is almost pure cellulose, and its airy fibers burn fast because oxygen can reach every strand.
Things that are flammable.Sawdust: Fine sawdust suspended in air can explode, a real hazard in woodworking shops and grain mills.
Things that are flammable.Rubbing alcohol: Rubbing alcohol burns with a faint, nearly invisible flame, so you may not see a fire in daylight.
Things that are flammable.Cardboard: Cardboard is thick enough to burn slowly, and it is a common fuel in landfill fires.
Things that are flammable.Hairspray: Many aerosol hairsprays contain flammable propellants, so a spark near the spray can cause a fireball.
Things that are flammable.Lighter fluid: Lighter fluid is very volatile, and spraying it on a lit barbecue is a notorious cause of burns.
Things that are flammable.Dry leaves: Dry leaves catch quickly, and dry leaf litter is a primary fuel that carries forest fires along the ground.
Things that are flammable.Firewood: Wood needs to dry for a year or more to burn well, because wet logs waste heat boiling off water.
Things that are flammable.Nail polish remover: Acetone in nail polish remover evaporates quickly, and its vapors ignite easily.
Things that are flammable.Water: Water cannot burn because it is already burnt hydrogen: hydrogen plus oxygen gives water.
Things that are flammable.Sand: Sand is mostly silica, which is already oxidized, so it cannot burn and is used to smother fires.
Things that are flammable.Brick: Bricks are fired in kilns at over a thousand degrees, so a house fire barely affects them.
Things that are flammable.Glass: Glass does not burn, but it softens and melts at very high heat, and in a fire a window can shatter from thermal shock.
Things that are flammable.Steel: Steel does not burn easily, but it loses about half its strength at a high enough heat, which matters in building fires.
Things that are flammable.Ceramic tile: Tile is baked clay, already fired in a kiln, so it will not catch fire.
Things that are flammable.Stone: Stone does not burn, but moisture trapped inside can make heated rocks crack and even burst.
Things that are flammable.Baking soda: Baking soda is not flammable, and when heated it releases carbon dioxide, which is why it can smother small fires.
Things that are flammable.Salt: Salt is already a stable compound and will not burn, though it can smother a grease fire.
Things that are flammable.Concrete: Concrete does not burn, though extreme heat can make the water within it flake off in a process called spalling.
Things that are flammable.Marble: Marble is a form of limestone, and strong heat can break it down into lime but it does not burn.
Things that are flammable.Gravel: Gravel is loose rock and does not burn, which is why it is used as firebreak around buildings.

Things with a spring inside.Mattress: Innerspring mattresses can hold hundreds of coils, which are tied together or wrapped in fabric pockets to move independently.
Things with a spring inside.Trampoline: Mats on a trampoline are linked to the frame by dozens of steel springs, which store and return your energy.
Things with a spring inside.Pogo stick: The pogo stick's spring stores energy when you push down, and then it throws you back up.
Things with a spring inside.Clothespin: A clothespin's spring pinches the two wooden arms together, so a tiny coil does all the gripping.
Things with a spring inside.Click pen: The clicker's mechanism combines a cam and a small spring that pushes the refill in and out.
Things with a spring inside.Stapler: A spring pushes the strip of staples forward, and a second spring in the head returns the arm after you press.
Things with a spring inside.Mousetrap: The classic snap trap's spring-loaded bar was patented in 1894 by William Hooker, and it's rarely been improved.
Things with a spring inside.Slinky: The Slinky was invented by accident in 1943 when engineer Richard James knocked a spring off a shelf and saw it walk.
Things with a spring inside.Jack-in-the-box: Turning the crank plays a tune, then a spring-loaded clown pops up; the toy has delighted and startled children for centuries.
Things with a spring inside.Pop-up toaster: A spring pushes the bread tray up once a timer or thermal sensor releases the latch.
Things with a spring inside.Tape measure: A coil spring winds the blade back into the case, so it snaps back when you release it.
Things with a spring inside.Pillow: A pillow is soft filling inside a cover, with no springs, which is why it squashes down instead of bouncing back.
Things with a spring inside.Spoon: A spoon is a single solid piece of metal, wood, or plastic, with no moving parts.
Things with a spring inside.Plate: Plates are plain, solid dishes, and springs would only get in the way of your dinner.
Things with a spring inside.Brick: Bricks are solid and dense, which is why they've been used for walls rather than bouncing.
Things with a spring inside.Candle: Candles are solid wax, though some holders use a spring to push the candle up as it burns down.
Things with a spring inside.Towel: A towel is woven loops of cotton, and nothing in it is mechanical.
Things with a spring inside.Sponge: A sponge springs back to shape, but through its elastic foam structure, not metal coils.
Things with a spring inside.Pencil: A standard wooden pencil has no moving parts, though a mechanical pencil has a spring in its clutch.
Things with a spring inside.Rug: A rug is woven or tufted fiber, and there's no mechanism inside.
Things with a spring inside.Mug: A mug is a single piece of ceramic, so there's nothing inside but your drink.
Things with a spring inside.Bean bag: A bean bag is filled with small polystyrene beads, which shift around so it molds to you.
Things with a spring inside.Hammock: A hammock is stretched fabric or rope that cradles you, and its flex comes from the weave, not a coil.
Things with a spring inside.Ruler: A basic ruler is a flat strip, though a steel one can flex a little without coils inside.

Things usually made of metal.Key: The oldest known lock and key are from Egypt roughly 4,000 years ago, and they were made of wood, not metal.
Things usually made of metal.Coin: The first coins appeared in Lydia, in today's Turkey, around 600 BC, made of a natural gold and silver alloy called electrum.
Things usually made of metal.Paper clip: The paper clip is usually bent steel wire, and the familiar Gem shape dates from the late 1800s.
Things usually made of metal.Nail: When the Romans abandoned a Scottish fort, they buried about 875,000 nails rather than leave them for their enemies.
Things usually made of metal.Screw: Archimedes is credited with a screw for lifting water, long before anyone used screws as fasteners.
Things usually made of metal.Saucepan: Copper conducts heat best, but most saucepans are stainless steel or aluminum, which cost less and last.
Things usually made of metal.Tin can: A tin can is really steel coated with a thin layer of tin, and canned food was invented before the can opener.
Things usually made of metal.Padlock: The Romans made padlocks, and those from ancient times have been found in Roman forts.
Things usually made of metal.Safety pin: Walter Hunt reportedly invented the safety pin in 1849 to pay off a $15 debt, and he sold the patent for $400.
Things usually made of metal.Thimble: The word comes from the Old English for a thumb-cover, and thimbles have been made of metal, bone and even leather.
Things usually made of metal.Anchor: Ancient ships used stone anchors, and a good iron anchor holds by digging into the seabed, not just by weight.
Things usually made of metal.Horseshoe: Lucky horseshoes are traditionally hung with the ends up so the luck cannot spill out.
Things usually made of metal.Bobby pin: Bobby pins got their name from the 1920s craze for bobbed hair, which they were invented to hold in place.
Things usually made of metal.Pencil: The pencil's cylinder is wood, but a small metal ferrule holds the eraser, and the lead is actually graphite.
Things usually made of metal.Eraser: Many modern erasers are vinyl rather than rubber, which makes them softer and cleaner on paper.
Things usually made of metal.Candle: Candles are wax around a cotton wick, and the wax is paraffin, beeswax or soy, never metal.
Things usually made of metal.Pillow: Down pillows are stuffed with the soft undercoating of ducks and geese, ideal for a cozy night.
Things usually made of metal.Sponge: Many kitchen sponges are cellulose from wood pulp, and the old natural sea sponge is a living animal's skeleton.
Things usually made of metal.Rubber duck: Bath ducks are plastic or vinyl, and Ernie from Sesame Street sang 'Rubber Duckie' in 1970.
Things usually made of metal.Sock: Wool socks keep feet warm even when damp, a quality no metal can claim.
Things usually made of metal.Teacup: Teacups are porcelain or ceramic, and handles were a European addition to Chinese tea bowls, which had none.
Things usually made of metal.Towel: Terry towels get their absorbency from thousands of cotton loops, not from anything metallic.
Things usually made of metal.Cork: Cork is bark from the cork oak, harvested about every nine years without cutting down the tree.
Things usually made of metal.Cardboard box: Corrugated cardboard was first used in the 1850s to line tall hats, long before it was used for shipping.

Tools for opening things.Can opener: Tin cans date from the 1810s, but the can opener only came decades later, and soldiers used bayonets in between.
Tools for opening things.Bottle opener: William Painter invented the crown cork bottle cap in 1892, and the bottle opener followed to pry it off.
Tools for opening things.Corkscrew: The waiter's friend corkscrew is a bottle opener, foil cutter and lever all in one pocket-sized tool.
Tools for opening things.Letter opener: A letter opener is a blunt blade used to slit envelopes cleanly, once a fixture of every desk.
Tools for opening things.Key: A key opens a lock by lifting its pins to the right heights, and the oldest known keys are about 4,000 years old.
Tools for opening things.Crowbar: A crowbar is a lever, so the longer the bar, the more force it can multiply to pry things open.
Tools for opening things.Box cutter: The box cutter's snap-off blade segments were inspired by a chocolate bar, according to inventor Yoshio Okada.
Tools for opening things.Jar opener: Jar openers give grip and leverage to break the vacuum seal that holds a lid tight.
Tools for opening things.Nutcracker: Nutcrackers use leverage to crack shells, and the famous wooden soldier nutcracker is a German tradition.
Tools for opening things.Oyster knife: An oyster knife has a short, sturdy blade, which pries the shell hinge apart without slicing the shucker.
Tools for opening things.Garage door opener: Remote-controlled garage door openers appeared in the 1920s, and radio controls came later.
Tools for opening things.Seam ripper: A seam ripper opens stitches with a small hook and blade, and it is the sewer's way to undo a mistake.
Tools for opening things.Stapler: A stapler fastens papers together, so it closes things rather than opens them.
Tools for opening things.Glue gun: A glue gun melts sticks of hot glue to join things, and it does the opposite of opening.
Tools for opening things.Sticky tape: Sticky tape joins and seals, and it does not open anything.
Tools for opening things.Zip tie: A zip tie locks with a ratchet and cannot be loosened, so it has to be cut off.
Tools for opening things.Padlock: A padlock keeps things shut, so it is the opposite of an opener.
Tools for opening things.Cork: A cork seals a bottle, so it closes things instead of opening them.
Tools for opening things.Bottle cap: A bottle cap is what the opener removes, and it is the thing being opened.
Tools for opening things.Twist tie: A twist tie seals a bag, so it holds things closed.
Tools for opening things.Bulldog clip: A bulldog clip holds papers together with spring tension, so it closes rather than opens.
Tools for opening things.Rubber band: A rubber band holds things together, so it is a closing tool.
Tools for opening things.Bag clip: A bag clip keeps snack bags shut, which is the opposite of opening.
Tools for opening things.Wax seal: A wax seal closed letters in the past, and breaking it showed someone had opened the letter.

Things you'd keep in a safe.Passport: Keeping your passport in a safe prevents loss or theft, and replacing one abroad can take days and cost a lot of money.
Things you'd keep in a safe.Jewelry: Jewelry is a classic safe item, and thieves are said to go for the bedroom first, so a hidden safe is a good idea.
Things you'd keep in a safe.Cash: Cash is the best known thing in safes, though most insurers limit what they will cover for cash stolen at home.
Things you'd keep in a safe.Birth certificate: A birth certificate is hard to replace and needed for passports, so it is among the most important papers in a safe.
Things you'd keep in a safe.Last will: A last will should be easy to find after you die, but a safe is only helpful if someone you trust knows the combination.
Things you'd keep in a safe.Gold bars: A standard gold bar in banking weighs about 400 troy ounces, roughly 27 pounds, and it is worth hundreds of thousands of dollars.
Things you'd keep in a safe.House deeds: House deeds prove ownership of property, and while copies exist at the land registry, many people keep the originals safe.
Things you'd keep in a safe.Family heirloom: Heirlooms carry sentimental value that insurance can't replace, which is why they're best kept in a safe.
Things you'd keep in a safe.Rare coins: Rare coins can be worth thousands, and handling them with bare fingers can leave marks that reduce their value.
Things you'd keep in a safe.Diamond ring: Diamonds are the hardest natural material, but they can chip, so storing them in a safe keeps them from scratching other items.
Things you'd keep in a safe.Savings bonds: Savings bonds are certificates of debt, and some old paper ones are cashable even decades after they were bought.
Things you'd keep in a safe.Bananas: Bananas ripen faster in a closed space because they give off ethylene gas, so a safe would turn them to mush.
Things you'd keep in a safe.Milk: Milk goes sour in hours at room temperature, and a safe has no cooling, so it's a recipe for a smelly mess.
Things you'd keep in a safe.Goldfish: A goldfish needs water and oxygen, and a locked safe has neither; goldfish can live for over a decade in a good tank.
Things you'd keep in a safe.Ice cream: Ice cream melts in a safe, since safes provide no cooling, and fire safes actually hold moisture to protect papers.
Things you'd keep in a safe.Umbrella: An umbrella is awkward and bulky, and stored damp in a safe it would grow mold and could rust the contents.
Things you'd keep in a safe.Broom: A broom is too long for a safe, and the cheapest item in the house doesn't need security at all.
Things you'd keep in a safe.Dirty laundry: Dirty laundry belongs in a hamper, and in a closed safe damp clothes would grow mildew and smell.
Things you'd keep in a safe.Bread: Bread goes stale and moldy in a closed box, and a safe is meant to protect valuables, not groceries.
Things you'd keep in a safe.Trash bag: A trash bag is for things you don't value, so it's the opposite of what a safe is for.
Things you'd keep in a safe.Old newspapers: Old newspapers are worth little, though a few historic front pages are valued by collectors, who store them in archival sleeves.
Things you'd keep in a safe.Houseplant: A houseplant needs sunlight and water, and a safe is dark and sealed, so it would wilt within weeks.
Things you'd keep in a safe.Toilet brush: A toilet brush isn't a valuable, and it would make a sealed safe unpleasant, so it's an unlikely safe item.
Things you'd keep in a safe.Raw fish: Raw fish spoils within a day at room temperature, and sealed in a safe it would become a smelly disaster.

Buttons on a TV remote.Volume up: Volume rockers are among the most-pressed buttons on any remote, and the 1956 Zenith Space Command was the first to use ultrasound.
Buttons on a TV remote.Mute: The mute key was a late addition; early remotes only changed channels, and today it silences the sound but not the subtitles.
Buttons on a TV remote.Power: Pressing power usually sets the TV to standby, which still draws a trickle of electricity, so a hard off saves more.
Buttons on a TV remote.Channel up: The channel buttons are a relic of the broadcast era, and some streaming boxes now skip them.
Buttons on a TV remote.Menu: The menu button opens settings for picture and sound, and many remotes hide a long press for a service menu.
Buttons on a TV remote.Guide: The program guide shows what is on, and its on-screen grid replaced printed TV listings.
Buttons on a TV remote.Input: The input key switches among HDMI ports, game consoles and antenna, and it saves a trip behind the set.
Buttons on a TV remote.Play: The triangle play symbol comes from tape recorders and points in the direction of tape travel.
Buttons on a TV remote.Pause: The two bars of pause date to tape decks, and a TV with a built-in recorder can pause live broadcasts.
Buttons on a TV remote.Rewind: The double left arrow is a tape-era icon, and streaming makes a 10-second skip back more useful.
Buttons on a TV remote.Fast forward: The double right arrow moves the tape ahead, and on a DVR it can speed through ads.
Buttons on a TV remote.Subtitles: Many viewers who are not hard of hearing now keep subtitles on, to follow mumbled dialogue and quiet scenes.
Buttons on a TV remote.Print: A trap: Print is a keyboard key, and TV remotes have no printer to talk to.
Buttons on a TV remote.Save: Save is a computer command, whereas a TV just plays what is broadcast.
Buttons on a TV remote.Copy: Copy is a computer command, and a TV has nothing to copy; the Ctrl-C shortcut is one of the most used key combos on earth.
Buttons on a TV remote.Paste: The paste command comes from cut and paste in the days of printed paper, using literal scissors and glue.
Buttons on a TV remote.Undo: Undo is mostly a software command, and the shortcut ctrl-Z was established in early graphical interfaces.
Buttons on a TV remote.Shift: Shift is a keyboard key whose name comes from the typewriter's carriage shifting upward to type capitals.
Buttons on a TV remote.Caps Lock: The Caps Lock key began as a typewriter's shift lock, and remains on almost every computer keyboard.
Buttons on a TV remote.Tab: The tab key comes from tabulate, from typewriters that set columns for tables.
Buttons on a TV remote.Escape: The escape key was added in the 1960s, and it let programmers break out of a running sequence.
Buttons on a TV remote.Spin: Spin belongs on a washing machine, where the drum whirls water from clothes.
Buttons on a TV remote.Defrost: This is a microwave button, whereas a TV never needs to thaw anything.
Buttons on a TV remote.Pulse: Pulse is a blender button for short bursts, which has no place on a TV remote.

Things made of cardboard.Cereal box: Cereal boxes are made of paperboard, which is thinner than corrugated cardboard but made of the same wood fiber.
Things made of cardboard.Shoebox: A shoebox is an object so beloved by kids that it has launched many school dioramas.
Things made of cardboard.Toilet roll tube: A toilet roll tube is a favorite craft material, and many cats love sitting in the cardboard, too.
Things made of cardboard.Pizza box: Pizza boxes use corrugated cardboard, whose wavy middle layer insulates the pie and soaks up some steam.
Things made of cardboard.Moving box: A moving box is often corrugated, and its fluted layer gives surprising strength for its weight.
Things made of cardboard.Paper towel tube: A paper towel tube is a craft staple, and it's recyclable cardboard.
Things made of cardboard.Coffee cup sleeve: Coffee cup sleeves were invented in 1993 by Jay Sorensen, after he burned his hand on a hot cup.
Things made of cardboard.Board game box: Board game boxes need sturdy cardboard to hold the weight of pieces stacked in a closet.
Things made of cardboard.Jigsaw puzzle piece: Jigsaw puzzle pieces are cut from thick cardboard, and early puzzles were hand cut from wood.
Things made of cardboard.Tissue box: Tissue boxes are made of paperboard, with a plastic film window for the tissue to pop through.
Things made of cardboard.Toothpaste box: Toothpaste boxes are mostly cardboard, and some brands cut out the box entirely to save waste.
Things made of cardboard.Hardcover: A hardcover book gets its stiff cover from cardboard wrapped in cloth or paper.
Things made of cardboard.Plastic bottle: A plastic bottle is a polymer, and it takes hundreds of years to break down in the environment.
Things made of cardboard.Tin can: A tin can is steel coated with tin, so it's a metal, not cardboard.
Things made of cardboard.Glass jar: A glass jar is made from sand and can be recycled endlessly with no loss in quality.
Things made of cardboard.Bubble wrap: Bubble wrap was originally invented in 1957 as textured wallpaper, and it's plastic.
Things made of cardboard.Styrofoam cup: A Styrofoam cup is a foam plastic, the opposite of cardboard in recyclability.
Things made of cardboard.Foil tray: A foil tray is aluminum, and it can be recycled if it's clean.
Things made of cardboard.Plastic bag: A plastic bag is made of polyethylene, which is a very different material from cardboard.
Things made of cardboard.Wooden crate: A wooden crate is lumber, which is stronger than cardboard but also heavier.
Things made of cardboard.Paper napkin: A paper napkin is thin tissue paper, not stiff enough to count as cardboard.
Things made of cardboard.Envelope: An envelope is thin paper, and cardboard is paper that is thick and layered.
Things made of cardboard.Receipt: A receipt is thermal paper, often coated with chemicals that make it hard to recycle.
Things made of cardboard.Ceramic mug: A ceramic mug is fired clay, so it's heavy and breakable, unlike cardboard.

Hospital departments.Emergency: Emergency rooms sort patients by triage, so a sprained ankle can wait while a later arrival with chest pain is seen first.
Hospital departments.Radiology: Wilhelm Röntgen's 1895 X-ray of his wife's hand, wedding ring and all, launched this specialty within a matter of months.
Hospital departments.Pediatrics: The word comes from Greek for 'child healer', and doses are calculated by weight because children are not small adults.
Hospital departments.Cardiology: A heart beats about 100,000 times a day, and cardiologists read its electrical rhythm as the wavy lines of an ECG.
Hospital departments.Oncology: The name comes from the Greek 'onkos', meaning mass or lump, which is how ancient doctors described tumors.
Hospital departments.Maternity: Newborns and mothers usually get matching wristbands, so no baby can be mixed up in the nursery.
Hospital departments.Neurology: Neurologists study a nervous system whose brain alone holds roughly 86 billion neurons.
Hospital departments.Orthopedics: Nicolas Andry coined it in 1741 from Greek for 'straight child', and a tree tied to a stake became the field's emblem.
Hospital departments.ICU: Intensive care often allots one nurse to just one or two patients, far richer staffing than an ordinary ward.
Hospital departments.Surgery: Before anesthesia, speed was everything: the surgeon Robert Liston reportedly removed a leg in under three minutes.
Hospital departments.Pathology: Pathologists rarely meet patients, yet their tissue diagnoses steer most cancer treatment decisions.
Hospital departments.Produce: A supermarket section, not a ward. Misters spray leafy greens to replace the moisture they lose after picking.
Hospital departments.Electronics: A store department. Hospitals do have biomedical engineers who maintain devices, but nobody sells them there.
Hospital departments.Menswear: Clothing retail, not medicine. Hospital gowns tie at the back so staff can reach patients lying in bed.
Hospital departments.Deli: Short for delicatessen, from German for 'delicacies', and a shop counter rather than a hospital department.
Hospital departments.Bakery: A shop department. Hospital food comes from a dietary kitchen, not a bakery, planned around each patient's needs.
Hospital departments.Toys: Toys belong to retail, though many children's hospitals employ play specialists who use them to ease fear.
Hospital departments.Checkout: A store till, not a ward. The hospital equivalent is discharge, where you leave with paperwork and no receipt.
Hospital departments.Garden center: A retail department, but many hospitals really do have healing gardens, which studies link to lower patient stress.
Hospital departments.Hardware: A trap: in a store it means tools and screws, while in surgery it means the plates and screws left in bones.
Hospital departments.Footwear: Retail shoes. Hospitals hand out grippy socks instead, because slips are a leading cause of falls on wards.
Hospital departments.Cosmetics: A store counter, not a ward. Plastic surgery is a real hospital department, but it rebuilds as much as it beautifies.
Hospital departments.Housewares: A store department. Hospitals have housekeeping instead, which matters hugely for controlling infection.
Hospital departments.Frozen foods: A supermarket aisle. Hospitals do use deep freezers, but they hold blood plasma and tissue samples.

The 'Big 9' US food allergens.Peanuts: Peanuts are legumes that ripen underground, yet they cause some of the most severe food allergy reactions.
The 'Big 9' US food allergens.Tree nuts: Allergy to one tree nut often means reacting to others, such as cashews and pistachios, which are close relatives.
The 'Big 9' US food allergens.Milk: Milk allergy is an immune reaction to milk proteins, which is different from lactose intolerance, a digestion problem.
The 'Big 9' US food allergens.Eggs: Many children outgrow egg allergy by their teens, unlike peanut allergy, which usually lasts for life.
The 'Big 9' US food allergens.Fish: Fish allergy often first appears in adulthood, and it covers finned fish; shellfish are a separate category.
The 'Big 9' US food allergens.Shellfish: US law counts crustaceans like shrimp and crab here, while mollusks such as clams are not on the federal list.
The 'Big 9' US food allergens.Soy: Soy hides in many packaged foods as lecithin or protein, so it is easy to eat without realizing.
The 'Big 9' US food allergens.Wheat: Wheat allergy differs from celiac disease: one involves allergic antibodies, the other a gluten autoimmune response.
The 'Big 9' US food allergens.Sesame: Sesame became the ninth major US allergen in 2023, after the FASTER Act added it to labeling rules.
The 'Big 9' US food allergens.Rice: Rice allergy is rare, so it is not on the list, and rice is often a safe staple in allergy-friendly diets.
The 'Big 9' US food allergens.Corn: Corn allergy exists but is uncommon, so it misses the list even though corn derivatives appear in countless foods.
The 'Big 9' US food allergens.Chocolate: Chocolate itself is not a major allergen; reactions usually trace to the milk, nuts or soy mixed into it.
The 'Big 9' US food allergens.Strawberries: Strawberry reactions are often itchy-mouth irritation rather than a classified major allergy.
The 'Big 9' US food allergens.Tomatoes: Tomatoes can itch the mouth of people with pollen allergy, but they are not among the big nine.
The 'Big 9' US food allergens.Oats: Oats are not a major allergen, but they are often cross-contaminated with wheat during processing.
The 'Big 9' US food allergens.Chicken: Chicken meat allergy is uncommon, while egg allergy is far more common, and that one is on the list.
The 'Big 9' US food allergens.Beef: Beef is not listed, yet a lone star tick bite can trigger alpha-gal syndrome, a real allergy to red meat.
The 'Big 9' US food allergens.Apples: Apples can bother people allergic to birch pollen, since the proteins resemble each other, but they are not a major allergen.
The 'Big 9' US food allergens.Bananas: Bananas share proteins with latex, so latex-allergic people may react, but bananas are not on the list.
The 'Big 9' US food allergens.Mustard: Mustard is a major allergen in Canada and Europe, but it is not part of the US big nine.
The 'Big 9' US food allergens.Celery: Celery is a regulated allergen in the EU, yet it is missing from the US list.
The 'Big 9' US food allergens.Potatoes: Potato allergy is rare, so despite being a global staple it does not make the US list.
The 'Big 9' US food allergens.Honey: Honey is not a listed allergen; its real risk is infant botulism, so it is avoided for babies under one.
The 'Big 9' US food allergens.Garlic: Garlic allergy is unusual, so it is not listed, though raw garlic can irritate skin and stomach.

Things your body does involuntarily.Sneeze: Sneezes are reflexes you can't really stop, though the old idea that your heart stops during one isn't true.
Things your body does involuntarily.Hiccup: Hiccups start with a diaphragm contraction you don't control, and babies even hiccup in the womb before birth.
Things your body does involuntarily.Shiver: Shivering is muscles twitching rapidly to generate heat when you're cold, and it can raise your body's heat output several times over.
Things your body does involuntarily.Heartbeat: Your heart beats on its own, thanks to a natural pacemaker cluster of cells that fires electrical signals with no command from the brain.
Things your body does involuntarily.Knee-jerk reflex: The doctor's tap on the tendon is answered by the spinal cord alone, so your leg kicks before your brain even registers it.
Things your body does involuntarily.Gag reflex: The gag reflex shields your airway from choking, and it triggers when something touches the back of the tongue or throat.
Things your body does involuntarily.Goosebumps: Tiny muscles pull body hairs upright; in our furry ancestors this puffed up fur for warmth or to look bigger.
Things your body does involuntarily.Sweating: A person has a couple of million sweat glands, and sweat itself is nearly odorless; the smell comes from bacteria on skin.
Things your body does involuntarily.Pupil dilation: Pupils widen in dim light and also when you're interested or excited, something you can't consciously control.
Things your body does involuntarily.Blushing: Blushing happens when blood vessels in the face widen, and Darwin called it the most peculiar and most human of all expressions.
Things your body does involuntarily.Digestion: Your gut works around the clock without any input, and food takes roughly one to three days to pass through it.
Things your body does involuntarily.Startle reflex: Newborns show a version called the Moro reflex, flinging their arms out when startled, which fades after a few months.
Things your body does involuntarily.Wink: Winking is deliberate, unlike blinking, and for some people closing just one eye is surprisingly hard.
Things your body does involuntarily.Whistle: Whistling takes conscious control of your lips and breath, so it's voluntary even when you do it without thinking.
Things your body does involuntarily.Clap: You choose to clap, which makes it voluntary, even though audiences often drift into perfect sync without planning.
Things your body does involuntarily.Wave: A wave is a chosen social signal, so it's voluntary, unlike the reflexes that simply happen to you.
Things your body does involuntarily.Nod: Nodding is a chosen movement, and in Bulgaria and parts of Greece it famously means no instead of yes.
Things your body does involuntarily.Shrug: Shrugging is a voluntary gesture found around the world to show doubt or indifference.
Things your body does involuntarily.Jump: A startled jolt is a reflex, but a deliberate jump uses conscious muscle control, so this one fits only as a choice.
Things your body does involuntarily.Snap: Finger snaps are among the fastest human movements, happening in about seven milliseconds, and are entirely deliberate.
Things your body does involuntarily.Skip: Skipping is a conscious rhythm of step and hop, so it's voluntary, however instinctive it feels to kids.
Things your body does involuntarily.Point: Babies start pointing around their first birthday, a deliberate act that's a key step toward language.
Things your body does involuntarily.Hum: Humming needs your choice but not your open mouth: the sound resonates through your nose with lips closed.
Things your body does involuntarily.Kick: A kick is voluntary, but the knee-jerk reflex is the involuntary leg kick, which is why the two can look alike.

Terrible things to juggle.Chainsaw: Canadian Ian Stewart set records for juggling three running chainsaws, a real act that's as dangerous as it sounds.
Terrible things to juggle.Kitchen knife: Knife juggling is a classic circus act, and a good juggler catches by the handle every time.
Terrible things to juggle.Flaming torch: Fire juggling is centuries old, using wicks soaked in fuel, and it's still risky today.
Terrible things to juggle.Bowling ball: A bowling ball weighs 3 to 7 kilos, among the heaviest things jugglers actually use, and a drop can break a foot.
Terrible things to juggle.Cactus: Cactus spines are often barbed and painful to remove, so every catch would hurt.
Terrible things to juggle.Raw egg: Raw eggs are a comic juggling prop, since one drop means a mess, and a salmonella risk too.
Terrible things to juggle.Anvil: An anvil weighs 50 kilos and up, so juggling one is a cartoon gag, though strongmen do lift them.
Terrible things to juggle.Glass vase: Jugglers use unbreakable props, since glass shards would end the show fast.
Terrible things to juggle.Machete: A machete's long blade makes it hard to catch safely, and a juggler's hands have no room for error.
Terrible things to juggle.Water balloon: A water balloon drenches the juggler at the first drop, so it's a comedy prop for brave performers.
Terrible things to juggle.Watermelon: Comedian Gallagher built a career on smashing watermelons with his Sledge-O-Matic, and a juggled one would burst at the first drop.
Terrible things to juggle.Wasp nest: A wasp nest can hold thousands of wasps, so juggling one is a very impressive way to get stung.
Terrible things to juggle.Beanbag: Beanbags don't roll away when dropped, which makes them the traditional first thing a beginner learns on.
Terrible things to juggle.Juggling ball: Juggling is thousands of years old, with Egyptian tomb art showing it from about 4,000 years ago.
Terrible things to juggle.Juggling club: Clubs spin end over end, so jugglers count flips as a measure of skill.
Terrible things to juggle.Silk scarf: Scarves fall slowly, giving beginners time to learn the three-item pattern.
Terrible things to juggle.Tennis ball: Tennis balls bounce and roll, but their weight and size make them a good starter prop.
Terrible things to juggle.Hacky sack: The hacky sack was invented in the 1970s by John Stalberger and Mike Marshall in Oregon.
Terrible things to juggle.Juggling ring: Rings spin through the air like frisbees, and jugglers can toss them in a thin, wide stack.
Terrible things to juggle.Orange: Oranges are a great juggling prop, and their size and weight are about right for practice.
Terrible things to juggle.Foam ball: Foam balls are soft, so they won't hurt on a drop, and they're good for indoor practice.
Terrible things to juggle.Ping-pong ball: Ping-pong balls weigh just 2.7 grams, so they're very hard to juggle accurately, a challenge for experts.
Terrible things to juggle.Apple: Apples work for juggling, and some performers take bites as they juggle.
Terrible things to juggle.Rubber ball: Rubber balls bounce, so jugglers can do bounce juggling on the floor.

Things you'd find in a haunted house.Cobwebs: Old cobwebs look gray and fuzzy because the silk collects dust. Spider silk is remarkably strong for its weight, rivaling steel strands of the same thickness.
Things you'd find in a haunted house.Ghost: Ghost tales are ancient: the Roman writer Pliny the Younger told of a chained, clanking specter haunting a house in Athens nearly 2,000 years ago.
Things you'd find in a haunted house.Creaky stairs: Creaks come from wood and nails rubbing as boards flex under weight. Changing humidity makes old staircases louder, which is why houses seem to groan at night.
Things you'd find in a haunted house.Bats: Bats are the only mammals capable of true flight. Many species hunt by echolocation, and a small bat can catch hundreds of insects in an hour.
Things you'd find in a haunted house.Skeleton: A grown human has 206 bones, but a newborn has around 300 softer ones that gradually fuse together during childhood.
Things you'd find in a haunted house.Candelabra: A candelabra holds several candles on branching arms. Before electric light, a grand house burned hundreds of candles for a single evening's party.
Things you'd find in a haunted house.Coffin: A coffin is the body-shaped box for the dead, and the word comes from the Greek for basket. The tapered six-sided shape became common in Europe by the Middle Ages.
Things you'd find in a haunted house.Spiders: Spiders are arachnids, not insects, and have eight legs. Despite their spooky reputation, only a small fraction of species are dangerous to people.
Things you'd find in a haunted house.Suit of armor: A full suit weighed roughly 15 to 25 kilograms, spread across the body so well that knights could mount a horse and move quite freely.
Things you'd find in a haunted house.Dusty portrait: The eyes that seem to follow you are a real optical effect: a painted face looking straight ahead appears to look at the viewer from any angle.
Things you'd find in a haunted house.Secret passage: English Catholic homes of the 1500s had hidden priest holes to shelter outlawed priests. Builder Nicholas Owen designed many and became a martyr.
Things you'd find in a haunted house.Rattling chains: The clanking, chained ghost owes much to Dickens: in A Christmas Carol, Marley's ghost drags the long chain he forged through a greedy life.
Things you'd find in a haunted house.Bouncy castle: Inflatables are held up by a constant blower, and they sometimes get lifted by gusts of wind. They suit a birthday party, not a haunted mansion.
Things you'd find in a haunted house.Rainbow: A rainbow is really a full circle of light. From the ground the horizon cuts it off, but from a plane you can sometimes see the whole ring.
Things you'd find in a haunted house.Disco ball: Mirror balls bounce a spotlight into hundreds of moving dots. They defined the 1970s dance floor, which is about as far from a haunted house as it gets.
Things you'd find in a haunted house.Unicorn: The unicorn is Scotland's national animal. Ancient writers may have been describing rhinos, and medieval traders sold narwhal tusks as unicorn horns.
Things you'd find in a haunted house.Ball pit: A ball pit is a pit of colorful plastic balls, a playground invention from the 1970s. It is pure cheerful fun and nothing a ghost would haunt.
Things you'd find in a haunted house.Water slide: Water slides run a thin film of water to cut friction and send riders flying. They belong in a summer waterpark, not a spooky old manor.
Things you'd find in a haunted house.Petting zoo: Petting zoos let kids touch gentle farm animals, and handwashing afterward matters because the animals can carry germs. Cheerful, not creepy.
Things you'd find in a haunted house.Smoothie bar: Smoothie bars took off with the electric blender and health-food culture of the 1960s and 70s. Fruit is more sunny than spooky.
Things you'd find in a haunted house.Balloon arch: Latex balloons slowly deflate because air seeps through the rubber. A balloon arch is a party decoration, so it wouldn't be found in a haunted house.
Things you'd find in a haunted house.Sunbed: Tanning beds give off strong ultraviolet light, which health agencies classify as carcinogenic. They are a spa item, not a haunted-house one.
Things you'd find in a haunted house.Trampoline: Gymnast George Nissen built an early trampoline in the 1930s after watching circus acrobats bounce off safety nets. It's a backyard toy, not a haunting.
Things you'd find in a haunted house.Hot tub: A hot tub keeps water around 38 to 40 degrees Celsius, so it is warm and cozy. Haunted houses are famous for the opposite: sudden cold spots.

Things a dentist hates you eating.Candy: Candy sugar feeds the bacteria that produce acid and eat away at enamel, and sticky types stay on teeth longer.
Things a dentist hates you eating.Toffee: Toffee is sticky and hard, and it can pull out fillings and even crack teeth.
Things a dentist hates you eating.Caramel: Caramel clings to teeth in the grooves, keeping sugar against enamel for hours.
Things a dentist hates you eating.Lollipop: Lollipops bathe teeth in sugar for a long time, as the slow lick keeps sugar in your mouth.
Things a dentist hates you eating.Soda: Soda is double trouble: sugar plus acid, and even diet sodas are acidic enough to erode enamel.
Things a dentist hates you eating.Gummy bears: Gummy bears are chewy and sticky, and they cling to teeth, giving bacteria a long meal.
Things a dentist hates you eating.Jawbreaker: Jawbreakers can crack teeth, and they're also pure sugar that sticks around for ages.
Things a dentist hates you eating.Taffy: Taffy is so sticky that it can pull off crowns and fillings, so dentists dread it.
Things a dentist hates you eating.Cotton candy: Cotton candy is pure sugar and dissolves into sticky threads that coat teeth.
Things a dentist hates you eating.Sour candy: Sour candies are often both sugary and acidic, which attacks enamel twice.
Things a dentist hates you eating.Hard candy: Hard candy is a double risk: it's all sugar, and biting it can chip a tooth.
Things a dentist hates you eating.Celery: Celery is crunchy and fibrous, and chewing it stimulates saliva that helps wash away food.
Things a dentist hates you eating.Cheese: Cheese raises the mouth's pH, and the calcium and casein in it help protect enamel.
Things a dentist hates you eating.Water: Water rinses food away and, if fluoridated, strengthens enamel, which is why dentists love it.
Things a dentist hates you eating.Broccoli: Broccoli is full of fiber and vitamins, and it's a tooth-friendly vegetable.
Things a dentist hates you eating.Plain yogurt: Plain yogurt has calcium and no added sugar, and some of its bacteria are friendly ones.
Things a dentist hates you eating.Carrot sticks: Carrot sticks are crunchy, and chewing them scrubs your teeth and gums and boosts saliva.
Things a dentist hates you eating.Milk: Milk contains calcium and phosphates, and it's one of the best drinks for strong teeth.
Things a dentist hates you eating.Spinach: Spinach is rich in calcium and folic acid, which supports healthy gums.
Things a dentist hates you eating.Eggs: Eggs contain vitamin D, which helps your body absorb calcium and keeps teeth strong.
Things a dentist hates you eating.Chicken: Chicken is a protein with phosphorus, a mineral that helps rebuild tooth enamel.
Things a dentist hates you eating.Green beans: Green beans are low in sugar and have vitamins that benefit your gums.
Things a dentist hates you eating.Almonds: Almonds are low in sugar and high in calcium, and so are good for teeth.
Things a dentist hates you eating.Cucumber: Cucumber is mostly water and crisp, and it can freshen your mouth.

Things in a TV studio.Camera: Studio cameras ride on wheeled pedestals so operators can glide smoothly from shot to shot without a bump on screen.
Things in a TV studio.Teleprompter: The prompter shows the script on glass in front of the lens, so presenters seem to look straight at you while they read.
Things in a TV studio.Green screen: Green is used because it's far from skin tones. Weather presenters often see the map only on monitors beside them.
Things in a TV studio.Boom mic: A boom mic hangs from a long pole just above the frame, close to speakers' mouths yet kept out of shot.
Things in a TV studio.Studio lights: Studio lights hang from a ceiling grid and run hot enough to make presenters sweat, which is why makeup is always on hand.
Things in a TV studio.Earpiece: Anchors wear a small earpiece that lets the director speak to them directly, even in the middle of a sentence.
Things in a TV studio.Control room: The director sits in the control room and picks which camera goes on air, calling shots by number.
Things in a TV studio.Monitors: Banks of monitors show every camera and incoming feed, so the director can choose what viewers see in real time.
Things in a TV studio.Floor manager: The floor manager is the director's eyes inside the studio, using hand signals to cue presenters when the show goes live.
Things in a TV studio.News desk: A news desk is built to look good on camera, with a glossy top and a logo. Often the presenter's legs are hidden anyway.
Things in a TV studio.Makeup room: Studio lights wash out faces and cause shine, so presenters get makeup even when they wouldn't wear any in daily life.
Things in a TV studio.Jury box: A jury box is courtroom furniture. TV dramas build one as a set piece, but a real TV studio doesn't have one.
Things in a TV studio.Kiln: A kiln is a potter's oven. Cooking clay at over 1,000 degrees Celsius has no place in a TV studio.
Things in a TV studio.Hay bale: Hay bales belong on a farm. They appear in a studio only as set dressing for a country-themed show.
Things in a TV studio.Pulpit: A pulpit is the raised stand a preacher speaks from. A TV studio might borrow one as a prop, but never as equipment.
Things in a TV studio.Anvil: An anvil is a blacksmith's block, not a TV fixture, though cartoons love dropping them on characters.
Things in a TV studio.Car lift: A car lift raises vehicles so mechanics can work underneath. Cars get filmed on location, not hoisted in the studio.
Things in a TV studio.Fire pole: Fire poles are found in fire stations. A TV set could include one only if the show is about firefighters.
Things in a TV studio.Bunk bed: Bunk beds are for dorms and cabins. Sitcoms build bedroom sets, but not as part of the studio itself.
Things in a TV studio.Operating table: Real operating tables belong to hospitals. Medical dramas build fake ones, and the real studio has none.
Things in a TV studio.Pottery wheel: A pottery wheel spins clay for a potter. A craft show might set one up, but it isn't studio equipment.
Things in a TV studio.Loom: A loom weaves cloth on a frame of threads. A craft show might film one, but it isn't part of a TV studio's kit.
Things in a TV studio.Altar: Altars are for religious ceremonies, and TV studios only borrow them for the occasional drama set.
Things in a TV studio.Hot tub: Hot tubs are for soaking, not broadcasting, though a lifestyle show might set up one as a prop.

Real jobs (not made up!).Ice sculptor: Carvers work in near-freezing rooms with chainsaws and chisels, and a standard ice block weighs about 300 pounds.
Real jobs (not made up!).Golf ball diver: Divers wade into course ponds to retrieve lost balls, which are cleaned and resold; a single pond can hold thousands.
Real jobs (not made up!).Pet food taster: Sensory panelists judge smell, texture and appearance, since the pets can't give notes, and some companies keep human tasters on staff.
Real jobs (not made up!).Water slide tester: Testers ride new slides to check speed and safety before they open, which is more technical than the fun job title suggests.
Real jobs (not made up!).Lego model builder: Lego employs Master Model Builders who build giant sculptures for Legoland parks, some using hundreds of thousands of bricks.
Real jobs (not made up!).Crossword setter: Setters design the grids and clues; British cryptic setters often work under pen names, like the famous Araucaria.
Real jobs (not made up!).Ice cream taster: Dairy companies employ tasters who sample many flavors daily; one famous Ben & Jerry's taster reportedly had his taste buds insured.
Real jobs (not made up!).Professional mourner: Hired mourners go back thousands of years in Egypt and China, and the trade still exists in parts of the world today.
Real jobs (not made up!).Foley artist: Named after Jack Foley, Foley artists create film sound effects live: snapping celery can stand in for breaking bones.
Real jobs (not made up!).Mattress tester: Testers lie on beds for a living, and machines also do the job by pressing thousands of times to mimic years of use.
Real jobs (not made up!).Cloud polisher: A made-up job: clouds are suspended water droplets or ice crystals, so there's nothing solid to shine.
Real jobs (not made up!).Rainbow painter: Rainbows are light refracting through raindrops, not objects anyone can paint; each viewer sees their own.
Real jobs (not made up!).Moon janitor: Not a real job, though there's litter up there: Apollo astronauts left dozens of objects on the lunar surface.
Real jobs (not made up!).Shadow trimmer: Nobody trims shadows, though shadow puppets in Indonesia are made from carved, cut leather held up to light.
Real jobs (not made up!).Echo collector: Echoes are reflected sound, and you can't gather them in a jar, though acoustic engineers do measure them.
Real jobs (not made up!).Dream inspector: Sleep researchers study dreams in labs, but no one inspects them; the title has the ring of a fairy tale.
Real jobs (not made up!).Puddle ironer: Pure whimsy: ironing a puddle would just splash it, and it would evaporate on its own anyway.
Real jobs (not made up!).Sunset director: Sunsets get their colors from scattered light, so no director is needed, though film crews do wait for the golden hour.
Real jobs (not made up!).Star duster: Stars are huge balls of gas, and the dust we really see in space is cosmic dust, which nobody wipes away.
Real jobs (not made up!).Wind folder: Wind can't be folded; it's moving air, though meteorologists do track it very carefully.
Real jobs (not made up!).Thunder tuner: Thunder is the sound of air expanding explosively around lightning, and nobody can tune it.
Real jobs (not made up!).Rain sorter: Meteorologists classify rain by intensity and type, but nobody sorts drops by hand.
Real jobs (not made up!).Gravity checker: Geophysicists do measure local gravity with gravimeters, so it's the closest fake to a real job, but the title isn't one.

Standard HTTP status codes.111: The 1xx range is informational, but 111 isn't defined; 100 is Continue.
Standard HTTP status codes.200: OK: the request succeeded. It's the code you see for nearly every normal web page load.
Standard HTTP status codes.201: Created means a request succeeded and also made a new resource, as in a successful POST.
Standard HTTP status codes.250: 250 is a success code in email's SMTP, not in HTTP, which has no 250.
Standard HTTP status codes.301: Moved Permanently tells browsers and search engines that a page has a new address for good.
Standard HTTP status codes.302: Found is a temporary redirect, in contrast with 301, which is permanent.
Standard HTTP status codes.333: Not a real status code; the 3xx range is for redirects but 333 isn't defined.
Standard HTTP status codes.401: Unauthorized actually means unauthenticated: you need to log in or provide valid credentials.
Standard HTTP status codes.403: Forbidden means the server understood you but refuses to let you in, unlike 401 where you aren't identified.
Standard HTTP status codes.404: Not Found. It's the most famous error, and the myth that it came from a room 404 at CERN has been debunked.
Standard HTTP status codes.418: I'm a teapot: an April Fools' joke from 1998 for the Hyper Text Coffee Pot Control Protocol, and it stuck around.
Standard HTTP status codes.429: Too Many Requests means you've been rate-limited for hitting the server too often.
Standard HTTP status codes.500: Internal Server Error: something broke on the server side, and it's a generic catch-all for the server's own bugs.
Standard HTTP status codes.502: Bad Gateway means a server acting as a proxy got an invalid reply from the server behind it.
Standard HTTP status codes.503: Service Unavailable usually means the server is overloaded or down for maintenance.
Standard HTTP status codes.606: Status codes top out in the 500s, so 606 doesn't exist.
Standard HTTP status codes.620: There are no 6xx HTTP codes; the classes stop at 5xx.
Standard HTTP status codes.640: HTTP's classes run 1xx to 5xx only, so anything in the 600s, like 640, is not a valid status code a server should send.
Standard HTTP status codes.700: HTTP status codes only run from 100 to 599, so 700 isn't valid.
Standard HTTP status codes.705: 705 is outside the 100 to 599 range and so is not a valid HTTP code.
Standard HTTP status codes.777: 777 is a famous Unix file permission, but it isn't an HTTP status code.
Standard HTTP status codes.808: HTTP has no 808, though it sounds like the Roland drum machine.
Standard HTTP status codes.880: HTTP codes stop at 599, so 880 isn't real.
Standard HTTP status codes.909: There is no 909 in HTTP; the highest class is 5xx.

Real-life robots (not fictional).ASIMO: Honda's humanoid, introduced in 2000, could run and climb stairs, and it was retired in 2018 as Honda shifted its research elsewhere.

Real-life robots (not fictional).Atlas: Boston Dynamics' humanoid became an internet star by doing parkour and backflips, and a newer electric version is aimed at factory work.
Real-life robots (not fictional).Curiosity: NASA's car-sized rover landed in Mars's Gale Crater in 2012 and found evidence that the area once held conditions suitable for microbial life.

Real-life robots (not fictional).Pepper: SoftBank's humanoid reads basic emotions from voices and faces. It was sold in Japan from 2015, and production later paused due to weak demand.
Real-life robots (not fictional).Perseverance: This NASA rover landed on Mars in 2021 carrying the helicopter Ingenuity and is collecting rock samples that may one day return to Earth.
Real-life robots (not fictional).Opportunity: Planned for 90 days, this Mars rover kept working for nearly 15 years after 2004, until a giant dust storm silenced it in 2018.
Real-life robots (not fictional).Ameca: Made by British firm Engineered Arts, it is known for startlingly lifelike facial expressions and is built as a platform for AI research.
Real-life robots (not fictional).R2-D2: Fictional: the beeping astromech from Star Wars. Ben Burtt created its voice, and Kenny Baker famously operated it from inside the costume.
Real-life robots (not fictional).WALL-E: Fictional Pixar trash-compacting hero. It spends the first half hour of its film with almost no spoken dialogue.
Real-life robots (not fictional).Bender: Fictional foul-mouthed robot from Futurama, whose full name is Bender Bending Rodriguez and who runs on alcohol.
Real-life robots (not fictional).Baymax: Fictional inflatable healthcare robot from Big Hero 6. Its design was inspired by real soft robotics research at Carnegie Mellon.
Real-life robots (not fictional).C-3PO: Fictional protocol droid from Star Wars, fluent in over six million forms of communication and the only character in all nine Skywalker saga films.
Real-life robots (not fictional).Johnny 5: Fictional robot from the 1986 film Short Circuit, brought to life by a lightning strike. The famous catchphrase is 'Need input!'
Real-life robots (not fictional).Robby the Robot: Fictional star of 1956's Forbidden Planet, he was so beloved he went on to appear in dozens of other films and TV shows.
Real-life robots (not fictional).Rosie: Fictional robot maid from The Jetsons. The real Roomba later made a similar dream partly real, but Rosie herself never existed.

Robots in Futurama.URL: A police robot whose name is a pun on web addresses, he patrols with his partner Smitty.
Robots in Futurama.Robot Devil: Hell's robot ruler is skilled at striking deals, and he even demands to have his hands switched in one episode.
Robots in Futurama.Kwanzaa-bot: A gentle robot who celebrates Kwanzaa in a show that loves to mash together holidays of the future.
Robots in Futurama.Clamps: A member of the Robot Mafia, he tags along with Donbot and Joey Mousepad.
