Robots in Futurama.Crushinator: A giant bruiser of a robot whose name promises exactly what he does to opponents.
Robots in Futurama.Robot Santa: Robot Santa judges everyone naughty or nice, but his standards are so strict that he goes on a murderous Christmas rampage each year.
Robots in Futurama.Leela: A human mutant, not a robot, she is a one-eyed captain whose full name is Turanga Leela.
Robots in Futurama.Fry: Philip J. Fry is a human frozen in 1999 and thawed in 2999, who delivers packages.
Robots in Futurama.Professor Farnsworth: Hubert J. Farnsworth is a human scientist who is 160 years old at the start of the series.

Robots in Futurama.Hermes: Hermes Conrad is a human Jamaican bureaucrat, not a robot, and a limbo champion.

Robots in Futurama.Zapp Brannigan: A vain human starship captain who is always trying to romance Leela.
Robots in Futurama.Kif: A green Amphibiosan alien who works as Zapp's long-suffering lieutenant.
Robots in Futurama.Mom: The owner of MomCorp is human, even though her company makes robots.
Robots in Futurama.Scruffy: A human janitor at Planet Express with a rough but kind spirit.
Robots in Futurama.Morbo: An alien news anchor who wants to destroy mankind live on air, he is a monster, not a robot.

Novels by Charles Dickens.Oliver Twist: Published in 1837-39, it follows an orphan who famously asks for more gruel; Dickens drew on his own childhood poverty.
Novels by Charles Dickens.Great Expectations: Pip's rise from blacksmith's boy to gentleman is told in a book Dickens first published in weekly installments in 1860-61.
Novels by Charles Dickens.David Copperfield: Dickens called it his 'favorite child'; this semi-autobiographical novel follows a boy who becomes a writer.
Novels by Charles Dickens.Bleak House: A sprawling 1850s novel opening with London fog and a never-ending lawsuit, Jarndyce and Jarndyce, it also features an early detective.
Novels by Charles Dickens.Hard Times: Dickens's short 1854 novel set in the industrial town of Coketown attacks a cold focus on facts, and is his only one without London scenes.
Novels by Charles Dickens.Little Dorrit: A tale of a family tied to a debtors' prison; Dickens's own father was jailed for debt, and the book echoes that.
Novels by Charles Dickens.A Christmas Carol: This 1843 novella gave us 'Bah! Humbug!' and helped revive Christmas traditions in Victorian England.
Novels by Charles Dickens.Nicholas Nickleby: It exposed cruel Yorkshire boarding schools; the real schools reportedly lost pupils after it appeared in 1838-39.
Novels by Charles Dickens.Our Mutual Friend: Dickens's last completed novel (1864-65) begins with a body pulled from the Thames, and a fortune hidden in dust heaps.
Novels by Charles Dickens.Dombey and Son: Its full title is Dealings with the Firm of Dombey and Son; this 1840s novel follows a proud businessman and his neglected daughter.
Novels by Charles Dickens.Barnaby Rudge: Set during the 1780 Gordon Riots, this is one of only two historical novels Dickens wrote.
Novels by Charles Dickens.The Pickwick Papers: Dickens's first novel (1836-37) was published in monthly parts and made him an overnight celebrity.
Novels by Charles Dickens.A Tale of Two Cities: This 1859 historical novel opens with 'It was the best of times' and is set in London and Paris during the French Revolution.
Novels by Charles Dickens.Vanity Fair: Thackeray, not Dickens, wrote this 1848 satire starring the scheming Becky Sharp; the title comes from a Bunyan allegory.
Novels by Charles Dickens.Middlemarch: George Eliot wrote this 1871-72 portrait of a provincial town; the author was a woman writing under a male pen name.
Novels by Charles Dickens.Jane Eyre: Charlotte Brontë's 1847 novel about an orphan turned governess; she first published it under the name Currer Bell.
Novels by Charles Dickens.Wuthering Heights: Emily Brontë's only novel, a stormy tale on the Yorkshire moors, was published in 1847 under the name Ellis Bell.
Novels by Charles Dickens.Emma: Jane Austen's comedy about a meddling matchmaker is from 1815, and nothing to do with Dickens.
Novels by Charles Dickens.Moby-Dick: Herman Melville's 1851 whaling epic, American, was largely ignored in his lifetime.
Novels by Charles Dickens.Les Misérables: Victor Hugo's French epic about Jean Valjean is not by Dickens, though it was written around the same time.
Novels by Charles Dickens.Ivanhoe: Sir Walter Scott's 1819 medieval romance of Robin Hood and knights helped popularize the Middle Ages in the Victorian era.
Novels by Charles Dickens.Tom Jones: Henry Fielding's 1749 comic novel, much older than Dickens, is about a foundling's adventures.
Novels by Charles Dickens.Silas Marner: George Eliot's 1861 novella about a miser who finds a golden-haired child is not by Dickens.
Novels by Charles Dickens.Jude the Obscure: Thomas Hardy's 1895 novel about a stonemason's dream of university so shocked readers that Hardy gave up writing novels.

Things that are usually orange.Carrot: Carrots were originally purple or yellow, and the orange kind was popularised by Dutch growers in the 1600s.
Things that are usually orange.Pumpkin: Pumpkins are technically a fruit and are around 90 percent water, and the orange comes from carotenoids.
Things that are usually orange.Orange: The colour was named after the fruit, and before that English had no word for it, so people said "yellow-red".
Things that are usually orange.Goldfish: Goldfish were bred from a dull brown carp in China over a thousand years ago, and now come in many colours.
Things that are usually orange.Traffic cone: Orange is highly visible in daylight and against road colours, which is why cones and work gear use it.
Things that are usually orange.Basketball: The original basketballs were brown, and the orange one was introduced in the late 1950s to be easier to see.
Things that are usually orange.Garfield: The cartoon cat, created by Jim Davis in 1978, famously loves lasagna and hates Mondays.
Things that are usually orange.Mandarin: The fruit is named after the Chinese officials called mandarins, who wore orange robes, or so the story says.
Things that are usually orange.Apricot: The apricot is related to plums and almonds, and its name for the fruit's colour was borrowed for a shade of orange.
Things that are usually orange.Cheetos: The snack's orange dust gets its colour from food dye, which famously stains fingers.
Things that are usually orange.Orangutan: Their orange fur is thick and shaggy, and the apes live in the rainforests of Borneo and Sumatra.
Things that are usually orange.Clownfish: Clownfish are immune to anemone stings thanks to a mucus coat, and all are born male and some become female.
Things that are usually orange.Banana: A banana is yellow when ripe, and the fruit is technically a berry.
Things that are usually orange.Lemon: Lemons are yellow, and the tree can fruit nearly all year round.
Things that are usually orange.Lime: Limes are green, and they're often picked while unripe, though fully ripe ones turn yellow.
Things that are usually orange.Tomato: Tomatoes are usually red when ripe, and they were once thought poisonous in Europe.
Things that are usually orange.Strawberry: The red fruit's seeds are on the outside, and it is not actually a true berry.
Things that are usually orange.Grape: Grapes are green, red or purple, and dried they become raisins.
Things that are usually orange.Blueberry: Blueberries are blue because of a waxy coating, and the flesh inside is greenish.
Things that are usually orange.Eggplant: Its purple skin comes from anthocyanins, and some varieties are white, which is where the "egg" name comes from.
Things that are usually orange.Plum: Plums are usually purple or red and, dried, become prunes.
Things that are usually orange.Corn: Corn is usually yellow in the kitchen but can be blue, red, white or even multicoloured.
Things that are usually orange.Cucumber: Cucumbers are green and are about 95 percent water, which makes them among the most hydrating foods.
Things that are usually orange.Ladybug: Ladybugs are usually red with black spots, though some species are orange or yellow.

Liquids at room temperature.Water: Water's solid form floats, which is rare among substances, since most solids sink in their own liquids.
Liquids at room temperature.Mercury: Mercury is the only metal liquid at standard conditions, long used in thermometers and called quicksilver.
Liquids at room temperature.Olive oil: Extra virgin olive oil is cold-pressed from olives, with no heat or solvents.
Liquids at room temperature.Milk: Milk is about 87 percent water, with fat droplets suspended in it; homogenizing breaks those droplets up.
Liquids at room temperature.Vinegar: The word vinegar comes from the French vin aigre, meaning sour wine.
Liquids at room temperature.Honey: Honey flows slowly because it's a thick supersaturated sugar solution that can crystallize over time.
Liquids at room temperature.Gasoline: Gasoline is a blend of hundreds of hydrocarbons, and the octane rating measures its resistance to engine knock.
Liquids at room temperature.Bromine: Bromine gets its name from the Greek bromos, meaning stench.
Liquids at room temperature.Maple syrup: Maple sap flows only when nights freeze and days thaw, so sugaring season is short.
Liquids at room temperature.Rubbing alcohol: Rubbing alcohol is usually 70 percent isopropyl, which kills germs better than a stronger 99 percent solution.
Liquids at room temperature.Soy sauce: Soy sauce is pressed from fermented soybean and wheat mash.
Liquids at room temperature.Butter: Butter is soft at room temperature, but it's a solid, melting only near body temperature, which gives it its melt-in-the-mouth feel.
Liquids at room temperature.Glass: Glass is a solid, and the idea that old windows are thicker at the bottom because glass flows is a myth.
Liquids at room temperature.Ice: Ice is less dense than water, so it floats, which is why lakes freeze from the top down.
Liquids at room temperature.Sand: Sand pours like a liquid in an hourglass, but every grain is solid.
Liquids at room temperature.Table salt: Table salt doesn't melt until about 800 degrees Celsius.
Liquids at room temperature.Candle wax: Paraffin candle wax melts at a modest 50 to 60 degrees Celsius or so.
Liquids at room temperature.Gallium: Gallium melts at about 30 degrees Celsius, so a spoon of it can melt in hot tea.
Liquids at room temperature.Steam: Steam is a gas, and the white cloud you see is tiny water droplets.
Liquids at room temperature.Helium: Helium stays a gas until about minus 269 degrees Celsius, the lowest boiling point of any element.
Liquids at room temperature.Iron: Iron melts only above 1,500 degrees Celsius, which is why blast furnaces and serious heat are needed to pour it.
Liquids at room temperature.Sugar: Sugar melts and then caramelizes around 160 to 180 degrees Celsius.
Liquids at room temperature.Rubber: Rubber is a solid elastomer; Charles Goodyear's 1839 vulcanization made it durable.
Liquids at room temperature.Chocolate bar: Chocolate melts just below body temperature, about 34 degrees Celsius, thanks to cocoa butter.

Things with a crust.Pizza: The crust is the soul of pizza, and Neapolitan pizza dough rises for at least eight hours before baking in under 90 seconds.
Things with a crust.Apple pie: A good pie crust uses cold butter, which melts in the oven and releases steam that forms flaky layers.
Things with a crust.Bread loaf: Bread crust browns through the Maillard reaction, which creates hundreds of flavor compounds, and it's why the outside tastes different.
Things with a crust.Planet Earth: Earth's crust is thinner relative to the planet than an apple's skin, only about 5 to 70 kilometers thick.
Things with a crust.Quiche: Quiche is a French dish from Lorraine, and the crust is often blind-baked first so it won't turn soggy.
Things with a crust.Cheesecake: Many cheesecakes have a crust of crushed graham crackers or biscuits mixed with butter, rather than pastry.
Things with a crust.Baguette: French law once set the baguette's ingredients, and the crust's crackle comes from steam injected into the oven.
Things with a crust.Tart: A tart's crust is usually shortcrust, called pâte sucrée when sweetened, baked in a shallow pan with a fluted edge.
Things with a crust.Pot pie: Chicken pot pie has a crust on top, and some versions are fully enclosed in pastry.
Things with a crust.Calzone: Calzone is a pizza folded into a half-moon and sealed, so the crust surrounds the filling, and the name means trouser leg.
Things with a crust.Empanada: Empanadas are pastry turnovers eaten across Spain and Latin America, and the name comes from the Spanish for to wrap in bread.
Things with a crust.Soup: Soup is liquid, with no crust, although a few versions come in a bread bowl.
Things with a crust.Salad: A salad is usually raw and crisp but has no baked crust, and the word comes from the Latin for salted.
Things with a crust.Pudding: Pudding is soft and smooth throughout, and traditional British steamed puddings get a skin rather than a crust.
Things with a crust.Ice cream: Ice cream has no crust, though cones can hold it, and the first cones appeared around 1904 at the St. Louis World's Fair.
Things with a crust.Rice: Rice is usually soft and fluffy, but the crispy layer at the pot's bottom is prized as tahdig in Persian cooking.
Things with a crust.Yogurt: Yogurt is a smooth, fermented milk with no crust, and it's made by live bacterial cultures.
Things with a crust.Smoothie: A smoothie is a blended drink, and it has no crust of any kind.
Things with a crust.Spaghetti: Spaghetti is boiled pasta, and its name is the plural of spaghetto, meaning little string.
Things with a crust.Jell-O: Jell-O wobbles because gelatin forms a flexible network, so it has no crust.
Things with a crust.Mashed potatoes: Mashed potatoes are smooth, but a shepherd's pie baked on top gets a browned crust.
Things with a crust.Omelet: An omelet is folded egg, and a good French one stays pale and creamy, without browning.
Things with a crust.Oatmeal: Oatmeal is a boiled porridge that's creamy throughout, and its crust-like skin forms only if left to cool.
Things with a crust.Popsicle: A popsicle is frozen juice on a stick, and has no crust.

Things that are curved.Banana: Bananas are slightly curved because the fruits grow toward the sun, a trait called negative geotropism, while hanging from the stalk.
Things that are curved.Boomerang: Aboriginal Australians made boomerangs thousands of years ago, and only some types are designed to return, as hunting ones fly straight.
Things that are curved.Rainbow: A rainbow is really a full circle of light; from the ground the horizon cuts off all but an arc, and from a plane you can see it complete.
Things that are curved.Crescent moon: The crescent is just the lit sliver we see from Earth; the Moon is always half lit, and the rest of the disc stays dark.
Things that are curved.Horseshoe: Hung on a door, a horseshoe is a traditional lucky charm, and it matches the U-shaped hoof it protects, usually fixed with nails.
Things that are curved.Fish hook: Curved fish hooks date back tens of thousands of years, and early ones were carved from bone, shell, and even thorns.
Things that are curved.Croissant: Its crescent shape gets credit to an Austrian pastry called kipferl, and croissants as we know them arrived in France in the 1800s.
Things that are curved.Archery bow: A bow stores energy in its curved limbs when drawn, then releases it as an arrow, and some ancient designs were made by pairing horn with wood.
Things that are curved.Scimitar: The curved scimitar blade was ideal for slashing from horseback, and the weapon is tied to Persian, Turkish, and Arab warriors.
Things that are curved.Elbow macaroni: Macaroni's curve is named for the elbow, and the hollow bend helps it grip sauce for dishes like mac and cheese.
Things that are curved.Cashew: Cashew nuts grow dangling from a fruit called the cashew apple, and the shell contains a skin-irritating oil, so they're never sold raw in shell.
Things that are curved.Shrimp: A shrimp curls its body tightly when cooked, and the curve is also how it flicks backward to escape predators.
Things that are curved.Elephant tusk: Tusks are really enlarged incisor teeth, and they curve upward as they grow, and elephants favor one side like left- or right-handers.
Things that are curved.Pencil: A pencil is straight on purpose, and its core is graphite, not lead, which was named after the Roman word plumbago.
Things that are curved.Ruler: A ruler has to be straight to measure; the word itself comes from its use for ruling, or drawing straight lines.
Things that are curved.Chopstick: Chopsticks have been used in China for over three thousand years, and they're straight, tapered sticks.
Things that are curved.Baguette: A baguette is long and straight, and a French decree says traditional ones may contain only flour, water, salt, and yeast.
Things that are curved.Dry spaghetti: Dry spaghetti snaps into three or more pieces when bent, a puzzle that Richard Feynman reportedly obsessed over.
Things that are curved.Laser beam: A laser beam is as straight as light gets, but gravity or a dense lens can still bend it, and light can bend around black holes.
Things that are curved.Flagpole: Tall flagpoles are built straight and vertical, and the tallest in the world soars more than 150 meters.
Things that are curved.Arrow: An arrow flies straight thanks to its fletching, the feathers or vanes that spin it, though the shaft itself is also slightly flexible.
Things that are curved.Yardstick: A yardstick is straight at 36 inches, and its name comes from the yard, which was once said to be the distance from nose to fingertip.
Things that are curved.Toothpick: The straight toothpick is a tiny wooden spear, and older ones were once carved from quills or silver.
Things that are curved.Broom handle: A broom handle is a straight wooden rod, and witches in fiction made it famous as a flying vehicle.

Things that run on rails.Train: The first steam passenger line opened in 1825, and some modern trains, such as maglevs, float using magnets rather than touching their tracks.
Things that run on rails.Tram: Trams run along rails set in city streets, and the first horse-drawn versions appeared in New York in the 1830s.
Things that run on rails.Streetcar: The American term for a tram, and San Francisco's cable cars are the only moving National Historic Landmark.
Things that run on rails.Roller coaster: Wheels lock to rails on a coaster, and the earliest versions grew out of Russian ice slides in the 1600s.
Things that run on rails.Funicular: A funicular uses two counterbalanced cars on a steep slope, one going up while the other descends, linked by cable.
Things that run on rails.Mine cart: These small carts ran on narrow rails in mines, and their narrow gauge is part of why early railways standardized the track.
Things that run on rails.Locomotive: The first successful steam locomotive ran in 1804 in Wales, pulling iron and men along rails at about walking speed.
Things that run on rails.Handcar: Pumped up and down by a lever, handcars were used by track workers, and they're still raced in some places.
Things that run on rails.Subway: The first underground railway opened in London in 1863, and the New York subway is one of the biggest in the world.
Things that run on rails.Freight train: Some freight trains stretch over a mile, and the longest on record was about 4.6 miles long, in Australia.
Things that run on rails.Bullet train: Japan's Shinkansen opened in 1964, and in decades of service it has had no passenger fatalities caused by a collision or derailment.
Things that run on rails.Bus: A bus runs on roads with ordinary wheels, so it's no train, and the word comes from 'omnibus', Latin for 'for all'.
Things that run on rails.Trolleybus: Close but not quite: it draws power from overhead wires like a tram, but it rolls on rubber tires, not rails.
Things that run on rails.Hovercraft: It floats on a cushion of air with no contact with the ground, so it needs no rails and can cross water and land.
Things that run on rails.Ski lift: These haul skiers uphill on a moving cable and chairs, not on rails, though a funicular is the rail equivalent.
Things that run on rails.Escalator: A moving staircase rides on a chain loop with tracks, but it isn't a vehicle on rails, and the word was once a trademark.
Things that run on rails.Segway: A two-wheeled self-balancing scooter, it runs on any flat surface, and its inventor Dean Kamen unveiled it in 2001.
Things that run on rails.Taxi: The word comes from 'taximeter', the device that measures fare, and cabs have no rails to follow.
Things that run on rails.Tuk-tuk: This three-wheeled ride named for the sound of its engine is common in Thailand, and it steers freely on streets.
Things that run on rails.Snowmobile: It glides on skis at the front and a track at the rear, and was invented to cross snow, not rails.
Things that run on rails.Ferry: Ferries cross water, so no rails, though some historic rail ferries carried entire trains across rivers and straits.
Things that run on rails.Bobsled: A bobsled runs in an ice channel, guided by the walls of the track rather than rails, and can reach about 90 mph.
Things that run on rails.Go-kart: It has no rails, and the first go-kart was built in 1956 by Art Ingels in California from lawnmower engines.
Things that run on rails.Rickshaw: The word comes from the Japanese for 'human-powered vehicle', and the rickshaw is pulled or pedaled on roads, not rails.

Words hiding the word 'bus'.Omnibus: Omnibus is Latin for "for all", and "bus" is a clipped version, so the vehicle's name is hidden here.

Words hiding the word 'bus'.Busker: Busker comes from Spanish "buscar", to seek, and street performers seek tips.

Words hiding the word 'bus'.Blush: Blush has B, U, S letters but with an L between B and U, so "bus" isn't hidden.
Words hiding the word 'bus'.Burst: Burst has "bur" and "urs", and the S comes after R, so no "bus".
Words hiding the word 'bus'.Brush: Brush has B, U, S spread over R, and so doesn't hide "bus".
Words hiding the word 'bus'.Bonus: Bonus ends in "nus", and has B and U and S, but O and N come between the first two.
Words hiding the word 'bus'.Basin: Basin has B, A, S but not B, U, S; it hides "sin" and "as".
Words hiding the word 'bus'.Census: Census hides "sus" and "ens", but not "bus", and comes from Latin for "assess".
Words hiding the word 'bus'.Status: Status has "tus" and "sta", and no B, so no "bus".
Words hiding the word 'bus'.Abacus: Abacus has "bac" and "cus", and an abacus is a counting frame used for thousands of years.
Words hiding the word 'bus'.Campus: Campus ends in "pus", not "bus", and comes from Latin for "field".
Words hiding the word 'bus'.Virus: Virus ends in "rus", and the word is Latin for slimy liquid or poison.
Words hiding the word 'bus'.Focus: Focus ends in "cus", and in Latin it meant hearth, the centre of the home.

Things at a campsite.Tent: The first modern nylon tents appeared after World War II; before that, canvas tents were heavy enough that campers needed horses or wagons to carry them.
Things at a campsite.Campfire: Fires burn best when air flows beneath them, which is why a teepee or log cabin layout of the wood works better than a tightly packed pile.
Things at a campsite.Sleeping bag: Down fill keeps warmth for its weight better than almost anything, but it loses insulation when wet, which is why synthetic bags remain popular.
Things at a campsite.Lantern: Early camp lanterns burned kerosene or white gas; the Coleman company popularized pressurized gas lanterns in the early 20th century.
Things at a campsite.Marshmallows: Originally made with sap from the marsh mallow plant in ancient Egypt, today's versions use gelatin and corn syrup instead.
Things at a campsite.Camping stove: Many backpacking stoves burn a blend of isobutane and propane, which keeps working in the cold better than butane alone.
Things at a campsite.Tent pegs: Sand and snow need special long or wide stakes, and some campers bury a stick as a dead-man anchor when nothing will grip the ground.
Things at a campsite.Flashlight: Many people call it a torch outside North America; red-light modes preserve night vision, which is why astronomers and campers like them.
Things at a campsite.Pocketknife: The Swiss Army Knife was first issued to Swiss soldiers in 1891, and the original Victorinox company made sure each was assembled in Switzerland.
Things at a campsite.Picnic table: Table benches at campsites are usually built from rot-resistant wood, and the basic pattern of a trestle table dates back to medieval times.
Things at a campsite.Firewood: Campers are urged to buy wood near where they burn it, since moving firewood can spread insects like the emerald ash borer that kill whole forests.
Things at a campsite.Chandelier: Medieval chandeliers were simple wooden crosses holding candles; glittering crystal versions came later, and none would survive a tent pole.
Things at a campsite.Grand piano: A concert grand weighs around 500 pounds and holds more than 200 strings with a tension equal to about 20 tons, so it won't be going camping.
Things at a campsite.Escalator: The word was a trademark of the Otis Elevator Company, and Otis lost exclusive rights to the name in 1950, making it a generic term.
Things at a campsite.Revolving door: Invented in 1888 by Philadelphian Theophilus Van Kannel, it helps buildings save energy by stopping wind from blowing straight in.
Things at a campsite.Doorman: This uniformed building attendant is an urban hotel job, not a campsite feature; campers have to let themselves in, usually through a zipper.
Things at a campsite.Elevator: Elisha Otis demonstrated his safety brake at the 1854 New York exhibition by cutting the rope of his own lift, which made tall buildings practical.
Things at a campsite.Dishwasher: Josephine Cochrane invented the first successful mechanical dishwasher in the 1880s because servants kept chipping her china.
Things at a campsite.Photocopier: Chester Carlson's first xerographic copy in 1938 read '10-22-38 Astoria', and it took years before anyone would commercialize the idea.
Things at a campsite.Jumbotron: Sony's early huge video screen at a Japanese 1985 expo gave the name, and it's now used loosely for any giant stadium display.
Things at a campsite.Ballroom: Their sprung wooden floors help dancers and absorb impact, a luxury a campsite's uneven grass would never give.
Things at a campsite.Red carpet: Rolling out red for important guests goes back to ancient Greece, where the play Agamemnon has a scene about walking on a crimson cloth.
Things at a campsite.Butler: The role grew from medieval household officers in charge of the wine cellar; the word comes from the Old French for bottle-bearer.
Things at a campsite.Valet: Parking valets are a hotel and restaurant service; the word comes from French for a manservant, and campers park their own cars.

Aircraft that need a runway to take off.Airliner: A modern airliner like a Boeing 737 needs around 2 km of runway to take off fully loaded, depending on weight and heat.
Aircraft that need a runway to take off.Jumbo jet: The Boeing 747 'jumbo' first flew commercially in 1970, and its distinctive upper deck hump started as a freight design.
Aircraft that need a runway to take off.Concorde: Concorde flew at about twice the speed of sound, and its takeoff roll needed a long runway, over 3 km.
Aircraft that need a runway to take off.Biplane: Two stacked wings give biplanes plenty of lift, so they can take off from short grass strips, but they still need a runway of some kind.
Aircraft that need a runway to take off.Cargo plane: Large freighters like the Antonov An-225 used a runway of over 3 km, and it was the heaviest plane ever built.
Aircraft that need a runway to take off.Learjet: The Learjet, first flown in 1963, popularized small fast business jets, but it still needs paved runway.
Aircraft that need a runway to take off.Cessna: The Cessna 172 is the most-produced aircraft in history, and it needs only a short runway.
Aircraft that need a runway to take off.Spitfire: The Spitfire's elliptical wing made it a fighter icon in the Battle of Britain, and it took off from grass airfields.
Aircraft that need a runway to take off.Airbus A380: The A380 is the biggest passenger airliner, with two full decks, and needs a runway about 3 km long at max weight.
Aircraft that need a runway to take off.Seaplane: A seaplane takes off from water, using floats instead of wheels, so it needs no runway.
Aircraft that need a runway to take off.Helicopter: A helicopter lifts straight up with its rotor, so a patch of ground is enough and it never needs a runway.
Aircraft that need a runway to take off.Hot air balloon: Hot air balloons rise because warm air is lighter than cool air; the first crewed flight, in Paris in 1783, needed no runway.
Aircraft that need a runway to take off.Blimp: A blimp is a non-rigid airship held up by helium, and it can rise vertically from a mooring mast.
Aircraft that need a runway to take off.Drone: Most small drones lift vertically like helicopters, though some fixed-wing ones launch by catapult or hand.
Aircraft that need a runway to take off.Harrier jump jet: The Harrier could take off straight up by swiveling its jet nozzles, nicknamed the 'jump jet'.
Aircraft that need a runway to take off.Hang glider: Hang gliders launch by running off a hillside or being towed, so they need a slope, not a runway.
Aircraft that need a runway to take off.Paraglider: A paraglider foot-launches from a hill, so it needs a slope instead of a runway.
Aircraft that need a runway to take off.Rocket: Rockets lift off vertically from a launch pad, no runway needed, except for SpaceShipTwo which launches from a carrier plane.
Aircraft that need a runway to take off.Hovercraft: A hovercraft rides a cushion of air over land or water, and used to ferry cars across the English Channel.
Aircraft that need a runway to take off.Zeppelin: Zeppelins are rigid airships, named for Count von Zeppelin, and they lift off from a mooring mast, not a runway.
Aircraft that need a runway to take off.Parachute: A parachute is dropped from a plane, so it is used after takeoff, not needing a runway.
Aircraft that need a runway to take off.Osprey: The V-22 Osprey tilts its rotors upward to take off like a helicopter and fly like a plane.
Aircraft that need a runway to take off.Kite: A kite needs only wind and a string, and kites in China date back over 2,000 years, long before any airfield.
Aircraft that need a runway to take off.Weather balloon: Weather balloons rise to about 30 km before bursting, carrying instruments called radiosondes, with no runway.

Christmas movies.A Christmas Story: The 1983 film about a boy who wants a BB gun, and its marathon airs on TV for 24 hours.
Christmas movies.Arthur Christmas: Aardman made this 2011 film about Santa's son, and the story mixes high-tech sleighs with tradition.
Christmas movies.Scrooged: Bill Murray plays a TV executive visited by ghosts in this 1988 take on A Christmas Carol.
Christmas movies.Christmas Vacation: The Griswold family stages a disastrous holiday in this 1989 comedy starring Chevy Chase.
Christmas movies.Hocus Pocus: A Halloween film from 1993, with three witches, and not a Christmas movie.
Christmas movies.Casper: This ghost story from 1995 stars a friendly ghost and is not about Christmas.
Christmas movies.Frozen: It is set in a snowy kingdom, but the story never mentions Christmas.
Christmas movies.Ghostbusters: A 1984 comedy about ghost-catchers, and no holiday is in it.
Christmas movies.Beetlejuice: A 1988 Tim Burton film about a ghost, and it is not seasonal.
Christmas movies.Jaws: The 1975 film is set in a summer beach town, so it is the opposite of Christmas.
Christmas movies.Up: The 2009 film is an adventure with a balloon house, and it is not seasonal.
Christmas movies.Coco: Coco is set around Mexico's Day of the Dead, in the fall, not at Christmas.
Christmas movies.Toy Story: The toys come alive in a bedroom and the film is about a birthday, so it is not Christmas.
Christmas movies.Finding Nemo: An ocean adventure, and it is not holiday-related.
Christmas movies.Groundhog Day: It happens on February 2 each year, so it is not a Christmas film.
Christmas movies.Hop: This 2011 comedy is about the Easter Bunny's son, so it is spring, not Christmas.
Christmas movies.Halloweentown: The 1998 Disney Channel movie is a Halloween story, not a Christmas movie.

Items on the Seder table.Maror: Bitter herbs, often horseradish or romaine, recall the bitterness of slavery in Egypt.
Items on the Seder table.Charoset: A sweet paste of fruit, nuts and wine whose texture recalls the mortar enslaved Israelites made; recipes vary across communities.
Items on the Seder table.Karpas: A green vegetable, often parsley, dipped in salt water near the start of the meal, a hint of spring.
Items on the Seder table.Zeroa: A roasted shank bone recalls the Passover sacrifice; some families use a chicken wing or neck.
Items on the Seder table.Beitzah: A roasted or hard-boiled egg that symbolizes the festival offering and, to some, mourning for the Temple.
Items on the Seder table.Chazeret: A second bitter herb, often romaine lettuce, used alongside maror, especially in the Hillel sandwich.
Items on the Seder table.Matzah: Unleavened bread recalls the Israelites leaving Egypt too fast for dough to rise; baking must be finished within 18 minutes.
Items on the Seder table.Salt water: Represents the tears of slavery; the karpas is dipped into it.
Items on the Seder table.Elijah's cup: An extra cup of wine is poured for the prophet Elijah, and the door is opened for him near the end of the meal.
Items on the Seder table.Haggadah: The text that guides the seder; thousands of editions exist, including Maxwell House's free ones, given out since 1932.
Items on the Seder table.Afikoman: A hidden piece of matzah that children search for and bargain for, and the last food of the meal.
Items on the Seder table.Dreidel: A spinning top for Hanukkah; its four letters stand for 'a great miracle happened there'.
Items on the Seder table.Menorah: A nine-branched candelabrum lit at Hanukkah, not on the Seder table.
Items on the Seder table.Shofar: A ram's horn blown at Rosh Hashanah and at the end of Yom Kippur.
Items on the Seder table.Lulav: A bundle of palm, myrtle and willow shaken on Sukkot.
Items on the Seder table.Etrog: A citron fruit held with the lulav on Sukkot.
Items on the Seder table.Sukkah: A temporary hut for Sukkot recalling the desert wandering, not a Seder item.
Items on the Seder table.Hamantaschen: Triangular filled cookies at Purim, named for Haman; the Yiddish name hints at poppy seed 'mohn' fillings.
Items on the Seder table.Megillah: The scroll of Esther, read aloud at Purim.
Items on the Seder table.Latkes: Fried potato pancakes for Hanukkah, cooked in oil to recall the Temple oil miracle.
Items on the Seder table.Gelt: Chocolate coins for Hanukkah; 'gelt' is Yiddish for money.
Items on the Seder table.Gragger: A noisemaker twirled at Purim to drown out the name of Haman.
Items on the Seder table.Sufganiyot: Jelly doughnuts eaten at Hanukkah, especially in Israel.
Items on the Seder table.Shamash: The helper candle on a Hanukkah menorah, used to light the others; the word means 'attendant'.
